  • Queries that were previously impossible are now a single selection – Identifying the moments a fandom has canonized, or the frames that will function as memes for a specific audience, previously required a person with deep familiarity with the title watching footage, and it didn’t scale across a catalog.
  • Discovery no longer depends on manual scrubbing – According to Social Department, campaign discovery work that used to take 3–4 days now takes about 10 minutes with QuickSearch. The time a marketer spent scrubbing through episodes for the right moment goes back to higher-value campaign work.
  • Marketers reach candidate clips without composing a query – That removes the requirement that the person searching already knows the library well enough to describe what they want, the constraint that made discovery depend on the few people who had watched the show.
  • Archived catalog becomes addressable – Content that was effectively unreachable, because it was finished, archived, and invisible to metadata search, becomes usable for campaign work, and titles that stopped airing years ago can re-enter live cultural conversations.
  • Industry recognition – Social Department was showcased as a top startup at NAB 2026 and featured in the Entertainment Loft.
“The hard part here was never the search. It was working out what to search for: how you take something a great marketer does on instinct, about which moment lands and why, and turn it into criteria a system can execute a thousand times. We spent a long time on that. Working with TrackIt on a compressed timeline, we went from spec to a live demo at NAB. TwelveLabs gives us the intelligence to understand what’s inside the footage and AWS gives us the infrastructure to do it at library scale. Our job is to know what to point it at.”
— Jonathan Verk, Founder and CEO, Social Department
“Everyone in media talks about adding metadata to their libraries but tagging content doesn’t pay for itself. What I like about this project is that it closes the loop. It takes shows sitting in an archive and makes them useful for real campaigns, at a cost that makes sense to run every day. That’s the part the industry has been missing.”
— Chris Marchitelli, Vice President, TrackIt

What we learned

The following four lessons from the project stood out.

The hard problem was expressing judgment, not retrieving content

Retrieval is largely solved. What isn’t solved is specifying intent precisely enough for retrieval to be useful without an expert marketer in the loop. Most of the engineering effort went into defining what qualifies as a shareable scene or a memeable frame, tightly enough to execute repeatedly across libraries with different tones and audiences. That definition is the output of a standing evaluation program of numbered iterations, each measured against per-show ground-truth sets and a tracked baseline, that tunes the criteria against results rather than intuition.

A multi-model architecture on Amazon Bedrock

QuickSearch uses a multi-model architecture, with each model assigned to the work it fits best. Claude Haiku handles bounded, cost-sensitive output, and Claude Sonnet handles tasks where cultural recall changes the answer. TwelveLabs Marengo produces multimodal embeddings, TwelveLabs Pegasus provides scene-level video reasoning, and the Amazon Rerank model handles reranking. Amazon Bedrock made this architecture practical to build and run. Models from TwelveLabs, Anthropic, and Amazon are available through one API, so Social Department can change the model behind a task when measured quality moves, without building a new integration. Asynchronous invocation runs long video embedding jobs at library scale, and the Rerank API adds a relevance pass without separately hosted infrastructure. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails helps screen search input in the same service, and customer data stays within the AWS data boundary. Because Amazon Bedrock is fully managed, the team operates no model-serving infrastructure of its own.

Signal that decays needs its own architecture

Treating trend data as another input to the content pipeline would have failed, because the two have incompatible lifecycles. Recognizing early that library content and live culture are separate systems, with separate refresh rates, storage, and failure modes, was the decision the rest of the design depended on.

Clear layer boundaries made a multi-party project work

Social Department owned the pipeline architecture, retrieval system, and editorial criteria. TrackIt built and delivered against that architecture, and TwelveLabs supplied the video understanding models. AWS, with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, provided the infrastructure, model access, and solution architecture for the AWS components. Because each party had a clearly defined scope, the 8-week production timeline held.

Conclusion

We described how Social Department, working with TrackIt, TwelveLabs, and AWS, built culture-aware video discovery for entertainment marketing using its own pipeline and retrieval architecture. Several AWS components make up the layer this post describes. TwelveLabs Marengo handles multimodal embedding and TwelveLabs Pegasus handles scene-level video reasoning, both on Amazon Bedrock. Anthropic’s Claude models on Amazon Bedrock handle interpretation and editorial ranking, and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless handles hybrid retrieval. AWS Step Functions, AWS Lambda, AWS Elemental MediaConvert, Amazon Rekognition, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon SQS run the pipelines around them. The result is a set of single-action queries that return the clips audiences already care about, the lines they already quote, the frames that will work as memes, and the moments that connect to whatever is trending right now.

To get started with multimodal video understanding on AWS, explore Amazon Bedrock and Amazon OpenSearch Service. To learn more about the TwelveLabs models available on Amazon Bedrock, visit the TwelveLabs page on AWS Marketplace. To explore how the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center can help your organization, visit the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center page.

Acknowledgements: The authors would like to thank Katie Kenney, Pranay Duhan, Xiaoye Qian, Rinne Han, and Dahler Battle for their work on this solution. We would also like to thank the TrackIt and TwelveLabs teams for their support.

About the authors

item.title: Connect Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway to private APIs in…
item.description: Full title: Connect Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway to private APIs in a hub-and-spoke network with centralized inspection
item.content:encoded:
Connect Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway to private APIs in a hub-and-spoke network with centralized inspection

In many enterprises, a central network team owns every virtual private cloud (VPC) and subnet, and every flow between VPCs must pass a central firewall in both directions. Agents that call internal REST APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, must meet the same two requirements. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model.

This post shows a pattern that meets both requirements. The network team keeps ownership of every subnet, and traffic between the Gateway and your private APIs and MCP servers crosses the central firewall in both directions. It covers where to place the Amazon VPC Lattice resource gateway that the Gateway uses to reach private targets. It also covers who owns each piece, six configuration decisions, and the checks that confirm the pattern works.

We built and tested the pattern in the US East (N. Virginia) AWS Region (us-east-1), in a lab with three member accounts and a management account in AWS Organizations. The AWS CloudFormation templates, test scripts, test evidence, and reference material (address plan, full validation checks, troubleshooting, quotas) are in the companion repository. Use the pattern as a guideline and adjust it to your own account architecture.

Terms used in this post

  • Resource gateway: The Amazon VPC Lattice entry point into a VPC: elastic network interfaces (ENIs) in subnets you choose. Backends see its addresses as the source of each connection.
  • Resource configuration: A VPC Lattice object that names one backend (here, an internal load balancer or VPC endpoint DNS name and port) behind a resource gateway. You can share it with other accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM).
  • Managed mode and self-managed mode: The two private endpoint options for Gateway targets. In managed mode, AgentCore creates the resource gateway for you. In self-managed mode, you create it and give the target a resource configuration.

When to use this pattern

Use this pattern when all of the following are true:

  • A network account owns every VPC, subnet, and AWS Transit Gateway attachment, and shares application subnets through AWS RAM.
  • A central firewall in an inspection VPC must inspect traffic entering and leaving every VPC.
  • Application teams manage only their own resources and security groups.

Otherwise, one of the options in Table 1 fits better.

Table 1: When another option fits better.

Your environmentUse
The Gateway account can own subnets that reach your toolsManaged mode
Traffic between the Gateway and the tools doesn’t need central inspectionSelf-managed mode, as documented
Tools are reachable on public endpointsA standard Gateway target

We also considered managed mode in subnets that AgentCore owns, a resource gateway in each tool VPC or in the central endpoints VPC, and internet-facing load balancers with AWS WAF per tool. The alternatives write-up explains why each falls short under these constraints.

Design requirements for centralized inspection

  • The network account owns every subnet. The Gateway and application accounts build only in subnets shared to them through AWS RAM.
  • Every flow between VPCs crosses the central firewall, in both directions. The central firewall in the inspection VPC inspects the traffic between the Gateway and your private APIs and MCP servers.

AgentCore Gateway reaches private targets through a VPC Lattice resource gateway, and the two private endpoint modes place it differently. Managed mode creates it in the Gateway account, which fits environments where that account can own the subnets it runs in. Self-managed mode, as documented, places it in subnets with direct access to the backend, which fits environments that do not require inspection between the Gateway and the tool. This environment needs both conditions at once, so the pattern uses self-managed mode with one change. The network account owns the resource gateway and places it in subnets routed through AWS Transit Gateway, so every request and reply passes the inspection VPC.

Solution overview

Give the resource gateway its own VPC and subnets in the network account. Don’t share them, and keep backends out of them. Route them through the transit gateway so every request and reply between VPCs crosses the firewall. Share one resource configuration per backend with the AgentCore account through AWS RAM. Figure 1 shows the accounts, VPCs, and traffic path.

Figure 1: The network account owns every VPC and the resource gateway. The other accounts own only what they place in shared subnets. Solid lines cross the firewall in both directions. Step numbers match the following traffic path

Traffic path

  • The agent, in a shared subnet with no internet route, calls the Gateway URL. Private DNS on the Gateway interface endpoint resolves it inside the agent’s VPC.
  • AWS WAF, if attached, evaluates the request. The Gateway checks its resource policy and the inbound JSON Web Token (JWT), then picks the target and tool.
  • The Gateway gets an outbound OAuth token for the tool account and sends the request through VPC Lattice to the resource gateway in the network account.
  • The resource gateway subnets route to the transit gateway, which sends the traffic through the inspection VPC to the tool account’s internal Application Load Balancer (ALB) or execute-api endpoint. (Crosses the firewall.)
  • The ALB or Amazon API Gateway validates the token and forwards the request to the backend.
  • The response returns the same way. (Crosses the firewall.)

How does Gateway traffic enter the network account’s VPC without a transit gateway attachment in the AgentCore account? When you create a target, AgentCore associates the shared resource configuration with its own VPC Lattice service network. VPC Lattice then delivers connections from that service network to the resource gateway’s network interfaces in your VPC. AWS operates that hop, and from there your routes and firewall take over.

What this pattern doesn’t do. Check these limits against your requirements before you adopt it:

  • No payload inspection – Traffic is TLS end to end from the Gateway to the ALB, with a certificate the Gateway validates. The firewall sees flow metadata and the TLS Server Name Indication (SNI), not payloads. Request content is in the Gateway, AWS WAF, and ALB logs.
  • Some legs skip the firewall – The agent-to-interface-endpoint leg and the Gateway-to-resource-gateway leg don’t cross it. Neither do the token requests that AgentCore makes to each identity provider.
  • No end-user identity at the tool – With the client credentials grant, every call that reaches the tool carries the Gateway’s client identity. To trace a call to a caller, use the inbound JWT claims in the Gateway application logs.

Who owns what

Table 2: Who creates what.

One timeNew API on a connected ALBNew ALB or tool account
Network teamResource gateway and its VPC, subnets, and routes. Firewall rules. A default route from the tool VPC to the transit gateway for the ALB’s signing-key fetch. Gateway interface endpoint and policy. AWS RAM shareNothingOne resource configuration added to the share. A firewall rule if the range is new
Tool teamAn ALB certificate whose subject alternative name matches the target host name that the AgentCore team usesA listener rule (with jwt-validation) on their ALBAn internal ALB and security group, and an app client for the Gateway (client credentials grant, with a scope such as tools/invoke)
AgentCore teamGateway, inbound authorizer, resource policy, optional AWS WAFOne Gateway target per API or MCP serverA target, plus an OAuth credential provider for a new identity provider

A new operation or tool on an existing target needs no new target: update the OpenAPI spec with UpdateGatewayTarget, or call SynchronizeGatewayTargets for an MCP server. The repository’s build order lists the steps in each account and the values the teams pass to each other.

Prerequisites

  • An organization in AWS Organizations with resource sharing in AWS RAM enabled.
  • AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) 2.37.7 or later, or the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) 1.43.106 or later, for the certificateConfigurations parameter.
  • For the role that creates Gateway targets: vpc-lattice:GetResourceConfiguration, vpc-lattice:CreateServiceNetworkResourceAssociation, vpc-lattice:GetServiceNetworkResourceAssociation, vpc-lattice:ListServiceNetworkResourceAssociations, and vpc-lattice:AssociateViaAWSService, plus the bedrock-agentcore target actions. Check your service control policies (SCPs) if your organization doesn’t use VPC Lattice today.
  • A firewall in a central inspection VPC attached to the transit gateway with appliance mode enabled.

Key design decisions

The snippets are excerpts from the lab templates and use the lab’s address plan. RGW_NET is the resource gateway subnets (10.0.1.0/24–10.0.3.0/24), TOOL_NET is the tool VPC (10.12.0.0/16), and ALB_NET is the ALB subnets in it.

Decision 1: Put the resource gateway in a dedicated VPC in the network account

Create a dedicated VPC in the network account for the resource gateway, with subnets you don’t share and no central endpoints or backends. Route those subnets to the transit gateway. Keep one resource gateway per trust zone.

ResourceGateway:
  Type: AWS::VpcLattice::ResourceGateway
  Properties:
    Name: hub-resource-gateway
    VpcIdentifier: !Ref ResourceGatewayVpc
    SubnetIds: [!Ref RgwSubnetA, !Ref RgwSubnetB, !Ref RgwSubnetC]
    SecurityGroupIds: [!Ref RgwSg]          # egress 443 to application ranges only
    IpAddressType: IPV4

RgwRouteToTgw:
  Type: AWS::EC2::Route
  Properties:
    RouteTableId: !Ref RgwRouteTable
    DestinationCidrBlock: 10.0.0.0/8        # internal ranges go to the transit gateway
    TransitGatewayId: !Ref Tgw

Used only with AgentCore, the resource gateway consumes one IP address per subnet, so small subnets are enough. Two settings can’t be changed after creation, Ipv4AddressesPerEni and ResourceConfigDnsResolution, so choose them up front. Use Availability Zone IDs that VPC Lattice and your AgentCore features support. The lab layout lists them for us-east-1.

Decision 2: Create one resource configuration per load balancer, and share it through AWS RAM

Point the resource configuration at the internal ALB DNS name and share it with the AgentCore account. Don’t start the name with rcfg-, which VPC Lattice reserves.

ToolsResourceConfig:
  Type: AWS::VpcLattice::ResourceConfiguration
  Properties:
    Name: tools-account-a
    ResourceConfigurationType: SINGLE
    ResourceGatewayId: !Ref ResourceGateway
    ProtocolType: TCP
    PortRanges: ["443"]
    ResourceConfigurationDefinition:
      DnsResource:
        DomainName: internal-tools-alb-1234567890.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com
        IpAddressType: IPV4

ShareToAgentCore:
  Type: AWS::RAM::ResourceShare
  Properties:
    Name: agentcore-resource-configs
    AllowExternalPrincipals: false
    Principals: ["<agentcore-account-id>"]
    ResourceArns: [!GetAtt ToolsResourceConfig.Arn]

VPC Lattice delivers the connection to the resource configuration’s domain. AgentCore sends the target URL’s host name (for example tools.example.internal) as the SNI and checks the ALB certificate against it. The certificate’s subject alternative name must match that host name. The host name doesn’t need to resolve in DNS.

For private API Gateway REST APIs, point one resource configuration at the network account’s execute-api interface endpoint. Each API’s target uses its own URL, and each API’s resource policy must allow that endpoint through aws:SourceVpce. In our tests, a second API in another account worked through the same resource configuration with no network change.

Decision 3: Pass only the flows you need through the firewall

Your firewall needs two stateful allows: from the resource gateway subnets to the tool VPC on port 443, and from the ALB subnets to the identity provider’s host name on port 443. Session-based firewalls pass replies of an allowed flow. In the lab we used AWS Network Firewall with strict rule order and the default actions Drop established and Alert established. With these defaults, the firewall drops client-to-server packets that no rule passes, and lets replies through unless a rule drops them. The rule-order notes explain the semantics.

# Policy: RuleOrder STRICT_ORDER, StatefulDefaultActions [aws:drop_established, aws:alert_established]
pass tcp $RGW_NET any -> $TOOL_NET 443 (msg:"resource gateway to tool VPC"; flow:to_server; sid:100001; rev:4;)
pass tls $ALB_NET any -> any 443 (msg:"ALB to identity provider JWKS"; tls.sni; content:"cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com"; nocase; startswith; endswith; flow:to_server; sid:100010; rev:2;)

The first rule allows only the resource gateway subnets to reach the tool VPC on port 443. The second allows the ALB to fetch its identity provider’s signing keys (JSON Web Key Set, or JWKS), only from the ALB subnets and only to the identity provider’s host name. The tool VPC needs a default route to the transit gateway for this fetch to reach central egress. If your identity provider isn’t Amazon Cognito, replace the host name. Without this rule, in our tests, the ALB returned HTTP 500 and the agent received MCP invocation failed.

To prove replies cross the firewall, we added a drop rule for the reply direction preceding the pass rule:

drop tcp $TOOL_NET 443 -> $RGW_NET any (msg:"PROOF return path blocked"; flow:to_client; sid:100098; rev:2;)

Tool calls then hung until timeout, and the firewall logged to_client drops for sid 100098. Removing the rule restored the calls. Run the same test on your own firewall.

Decision 4: Validate the tool account’s token on the internal ALB or private API

The tool account keeps its own identity provider (Amazon Cognito in the lab) and creates an app client for the Gateway. Validate that client’s token on every path to the backend.

Internal ALB – Make the listener’s default action a fixed response, and put a jwt-validation action on every rule that forwards. Pin client_id to the Gateway’s app client so that other clients in the same user pool are rejected.

McpRule:
  Type: AWS::ElasticLoadBalancingV2::ListenerRule
  Properties:
    ListenerArn: !Ref Listener                # default action: fixed-response 404
    Priority: 10
    Conditions: [{Field: path-pattern, PathPatternConfig: {Values: [/mcp]}}]
    Actions:
      - Type: jwt-validation
        Order: 1
        JwtValidationConfig:
          Issuer: !Sub https://cognito-idp.${AWS::Region}.amazonaws.com/${ToolPool}
          JwksEndpoint: !Sub https://cognito-idp.${AWS::Region}.amazonaws.com/${ToolPool}/.well-known/jwks.json
          AdditionalClaims:
            - {Format: space-separated-values, Name: scope, Values: [tools/invoke]}
            - {Format: single-string, Name: client_id, Values: [!Ref GatewayAppClient]}
      - Type: forward
        Order: 2
        TargetGroupArn: !Ref ToolsTargetGroup

In our tests, a target with no token, one with another identity provider’s token, and one with a different app client’s token were all rejected with HTTP 401 before the backend ran. The agent saw only An internal error occurred, so use the ALB access logs to diagnose token problems.

Private REST API – An API key doesn’t authenticate the caller, so add an authorizer to every method, such as a Cognito user pool authorizer with a required scope (as in the lab). Also attach an endpoint policy to the execute-api endpoint that limits it to APIs owned by approved accounts. It controls which APIs the endpoint reaches, not who calls it. The authorizer controls the caller.

{"Statement": [{"Effect": "Allow", "Principal": "*", "Action": "execute-api:Invoke",
  "Resource": ["arn:aws:execute-api:us-east-1:<tool-account-id>:*"]}]}

The ALB or endpoint security group allows only the resource gateway subnets, so the resource gateway is the only network path in. If your firewall applies source NAT, the security group must allow the firewall’s addresses instead, and it then admits anything the firewall forwards. The firewall rule and the token validation become the controls.

Decision 5: Create Gateway targets that reference the shared resource configuration

Create the Gateway with a JWT authorizer and, optionally, an AWS WAF web access control list (web ACL), which inspects the tool-call arguments for every target. AWS WAF inspects only the first 16 KB of the body by default (adjustable to 64 KB), so decide how each rule handles larger bodies. Add AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet to the common rule set. See the AWS WAF notes.

Gateway targets with a private endpoint can’t use NO_AUTH for inbound authorization unless you configure an interceptor function.

Each target needs an OAuth credential provider that holds the tool account’s app client ID and secret and the identity provider’s discovery URL:

# provider.json holds the client secret, so it stays out of the command line and shell history:
# {"name": "tools-account-a", "credentialProviderVendor": "CustomOauth2",
#  "oauth2ProviderConfigInput": {"customOauth2ProviderConfig": {
#    "clientId": "<tool-app-client-id>", "clientSecret": "<tool-app-client-secret>",
#    "oauthDiscovery": {"discoveryUrl": "https://cognito-idp.<region>.amazonaws.com/<pool-id>/.well-known/openid-configuration"}}}}
chmod 600 provider.json
aws bedrock-agentcore-control create-oauth2-credential-provider --cli-input-json file://provider.json
rm provider.json

If the ALB uses a certificate from a private certificate authority (CA), also store the CA certificate as a PEM string in an AWS Secrets Manager secret. The Gateway execution role (the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role you give the Gateway when you create it) needs permission to read that secret and the credential provider.

import boto3

agentcore = boto3.client("bedrock-agentcore-control", region_name="us-east-1")

agentcore.create_gateway_target(
    gatewayIdentifier="<gateway-id>",
    name="classifier",
    targetConfiguration={"mcp": {"mcpServer": {"endpoint": "https://tools.example.internal/mcp"}}},
    credentialProviderConfigurations=[{
        "credentialProviderType": "OAUTH",
        "credentialProvider": {"oauthCredentialProvider": {
            "providerArn": "<oauth-provider-arn>",
            "scopes": ["tools/invoke"],
            "grantType": "CLIENT_CREDENTIALS"}}}],
    # Shared from the network account through AWS RAM
    privateEndpoint={"selfManagedLatticeResource": {
        "resourceConfigurationIdentifier": "<shared-resource-configuration-arn>"}},
    # Trust the private CA that issued the ALB certificate
    certificateConfigurations=[{"secretsManager": {"secretArn": "<ca-secret-arn>"}}],
)

An OpenAPI target uses the same blocks with openApiSchema in place of mcpServer. To rotate the CA, update the secret and call UpdateGatewayTarget. Open connections can keep the old trust material for up to 15 minutes.

Keep the Gateway the only consumer of the shared resource configuration. The AWS managed permission for AWS RAM also grants ec2:CreateVpcEndpoint, so the AgentCore account could reach the backend through a resource VPC endpoint or service network of its own. A customer managed permission can’t fix this: AWS RAM rejects vpc-lattice:AssociateViaAWSService in one, and without it Gateway targets fail. Attach an SCP to the AgentCore account instead:

{"Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [
  {"Sid": "NoOwnEndpointsToSharedResourceConfigurations", "Effect": "Deny",
   "Action": "ec2:CreateVpcEndpoint", "Resource": "arn:aws:vpc-lattice:*:*:resourceconfiguration/*"},
  {"Sid": "ServiceNetworkAssociationsOnlyThroughAwsServices", "Effect": "Deny",
   "Action": "vpc-lattice:CreateServiceNetworkResourceAssociation", "Resource": "*",
   "Condition": {"BoolIfExists": {"aws:ViaAWSService": "false"}}}]}

With this SCP, our attempts to create a resource VPC endpoint and a service network association of its own were denied, and a new Gateway target still reached READY. SCPs don’t apply to the management account, so don’t run AgentCore there. In the network account, alarm on unexpected associations with an Amazon EventBridge rule that matches the AWS CloudTrail event CreateServiceNetworkResourceAssociationBySharee.

Revoke access by deleting the Gateway targets (or the service network resource association) first, then removing the resource configuration from the share. Removing it from the share alone doesn’t remove existing associations.

Decision 6: Reach the Gateway privately, and close the public endpoint

Create the Gateway interface endpoint in the shared agent VPC with private DNS enabled, and attach an endpoint policy that lists the approved Gateways. The principal must be *, because the Gateway authenticates callers with bearer tokens. The Resource list is the control.

{"Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{"Effect": "Allow", "Principal": "*", "Action": "bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway",
  "Resource": ["arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1:<agentcore-account-id>:gateway/<gateway-id>"]}]}

In our tests, a second Gateway called through the same endpoint returned JSON-RPC error -32002 Insufficient permissions, but still answered on its public endpoint.

The interface endpoint doesn’t close the Gateway’s public endpoint. Attach a resource policy that allows bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway only when aws:SourceVpce is your endpoint and denies it otherwise (the full policy is in the repository). In our tests, internet calls returned -32002 about 30 seconds after we applied it, while endpoint calls kept working. AWS notes policy changes can take up to 15 minutes.

An agent with no internet route still needs its inbound JWT. Give it a path to its identity provider’s token endpoint, such as a route to the transit gateway and a firewall rule scoped like the JWKS rule in Decision 3. Alternatively, use a private identity provider.

Validate the pattern in your environment

Before you rely on the pattern, run these checks in a non-production copy of your network account, with your own firewall. The full list of 14 checks, with how to run each and the results we saw, is in the repository, along with a log source for every hop.

  • Requests come from the resource gateway – The ALB access log shows a source IP in the resource gateway range (or your firewall’s range, if it applies source NAT).
  • Requests cross the firewall – Firewall flow logs show TLS flows from resource gateway addresses to the tool account on port 443.
  • Replies cross the firewall – With a reply-direction drop rule in place (Decision 3), calls fail and the firewall logs to_client drops.
  • The ALB and private API are token boundaries – Targets with no token, or another client’s token, get HTTP 401 and the backend isn’t invoked.
  • The public Gateway endpoint is closed – With the resource policy attached, internet calls get -32002 and endpoint calls succeed.

If a check fails or the agent gets a generic error, the troubleshooting guide maps each symptom to the log that shows the cause.

Considerations

  • Cost: Each VPC Lattice service network resource association carries an hourly charge plus data processing. See VPC Lattice pricing. Plan for one association per target. To see how many associations your targets create, compare the resourceAssociationArn that GetGatewayTarget returns for each target, and prefer one target per API or MCP server over many small targets.
  • Traffic to public endpoints: Three calls leave the private path: the ALB’s JWKS fetch, the agent’s inbound token request, and AgentCore’s outbound OAuth token requests to each identity provider.
  • Account layout and quotas: Gateway tool-call quotas apply per account as well as per gateway. Use one AgentCore account per environment, and split gateways by domain or agent group well before the limits. VPC Lattice closes idle connections, so use keepalives for long-lived MCP streams. The repository lists the other quotas.
  • Scope of our tests: We used AWS Network Firewall, no source NAT, and us-east-1 only. Source NAT, multiple Regions, private identity providers, and OpenAPI limitations are covered in the other considerations.

Conclusion

When your network team owns every subnet and every flow between VPCs must pass a central firewall, place the VPC Lattice resource gateway in the network account and route its subnets through the transit gateway. The network team sets up the entry point once and adds one resource configuration per backend load balancer. Application teams keep owning only their load balancers, security groups, identity providers, and Gateway targets, and AWS WAF moves from per-tool public load balancers to the Gateway. Run the validation checks in your own environment before you rely on the pattern.

About the authors

item.title: How Stretto built an AI voice agent with Amazon Nova 2 Sonic
item.content:encoded:
How Stretto built an AI voice agent with Amazon Nova 2 Sonic

This post is co-written with Danya Gordin from Stretto and Marcelo Wzorek from CI&T.

Before Stretto built an AI voice agent, consumers considering bankruptcy on its Bankruptcy.com site filled out a web form with a few fields: debt amount, attorney status, and contact information. These form-generated leads carried thin margins.

The gap between a web form lead and a fully qualified lead is significant. Bankruptcy attorneys place more value on a lead that includes detailed financial data: debts, assets, vehicles, real estate, employment history, and prior filings. The web form could have been extended to capture that detail, but the longer it got, the more visitors abandoned it partway through. A phone interview would have drawn the information out naturally, because people are more willing to share financially sensitive details in conversation, but staffing and training a human intake team to run those interviews was cost-prohibitive.

Stretto saw an opportunity: replace the web form with an AI voice agent that conducts the intake interview by phone. The agent would guide callers through the full bankruptcy questionnaire conversationally and extract structured data in real time. It would then sort leads against attorney-defined rules to support attorney decision-making.

The challenge was finding a voice AI solution that could handle sensitive financial conversations naturally, with low latency, clean interruption handling, and emotional awareness, at a cost that made the unit economics work.

In this post, we walk through how Stretto worked with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center and CI&T (an AWS Partner) to build Tara, an AI voice agent powered by Amazon Nova 2 Sonic, a speech-to-speech model in Amazon Bedrock. Tara conducts multi-phase bankruptcy intake interviews and sorts leads against attorney-defined rules. We cover the architecture, the phased build from validation through production deployment, and how the team tested voice quality for sensitive conversations.

Solution overview

Tara is an AI voice agent that conducts bankruptcy intake interviews over the phone. When a caller dials the Bankruptcy.com number, Tara picks up, introduces herself, and guides the caller through a structured conversation. She collects personal information, financial details, asset inventories, and employment history while adapting her tone to the caller’s emotional state. At the end of the call, Stretto’s system applies attorney-defined rules to sort the lead as qualified, disqualified, or needs-more-information for attorney review.

The solution is built on Amazon Nova 2 Sonic, a speech-to-speech foundation model (FM)available through Amazon Bedrock. It processes speech input and generates speech output natively in a single model rather than chaining separate speech-to-text, language model, and text-to-speech components. This architecture is designed to reduce latency and produce more natural-sounding conversations, both critical for the sensitive nature of bankruptcy intake calls. Building on Amazon Bedrock gave the team both Amazon Nova 2 Sonic and Anthropic’s Claude through one managed service, with no model infrastructure to run. It also brought AWS security and governance controls to a workload that handles sensitive financial data. Access to both models is governed by AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Traffic to Amazon Bedrock stays on the AWS network through virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoints (AWS PrivateLink). Amazon Bedrock doesn’t use prompts or model outputs to train models (for details, see Data protection in Amazon Bedrock). Because the models run in the same AWS environment as the voice bridge, the database, and Amazon CloudWatch monitoring, the team could secure and operate the whole solution with one set of tools. Amazon Nova 2 Sonic and Amazon Bedrock are not available in all AWS Regions. For current Region availability, see Amazon Bedrock supported Regions.

The team chose Amazon Nova 2 Sonic over the previous voice solution for three reasons:

  • Cost: Stretto reports a 95 percent reduction in per-minute voice cost compared to its previous solution, based on Amazon Bedrock on-demand pricing in us-east-1 as of April 2026.
  • Latency: In Stretto’s testing, the previous solution exhibited time-to-first-audio latency above 500 milliseconds, creating awkward pauses. Amazon Nova 2 Sonic is designed for low latency to support natural conversational flow.
  • Interruption handling: Callers in stressful situations need to interject, correct themselves, and ask clarifying questions. The previous solution handled barge-in poorly, often breaking the conversation flow. Amazon Nova 2 Sonic is designed to handle interruptions without breaking the session.

The following figure shows the end-to-end architecture.

Figure 1: Tara architecture showing the end-to-end call flow from telephony to data persistence

A caller reaches Tara through Twilio, which opens a WebSocket connection into AWS. Traffic passes through AWS WAF and an Application Load Balancer to the voice bridge on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate, which streams audio with Amazon Nova 2 Sonic (accessed through Amazon Bedrock). After the call, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) with a dead-letter queue hands the transcript to an asynchronous processor. The processor uses Anthropic’s Claude 3 Haiku on Amazon Bedrock to extract structured fields, which persist in Amazon Aurora Serverless v2. Qualified leads route to attorneys by jurisdiction. Supporting services include NAT gateways, VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink), Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), AWS Secrets Manager, and Amazon CloudWatch.

Stretto used Twilio for telephony because Tara’s intake is fully automated, with no human agents taking calls, and because Stretto wanted a direct integration with Amazon Nova 2 Sonic that kept its existing AWS backend in place. Twilio Media Streams delivers the caller’s raw audio over a WebSocket, which is the input the voice bridge needs, and CI&T had already integrated it with Amazon Nova 2 Sonic. For contact center workloads that route calls among human agents, Amazon Connect also supports Amazon Nova 2 Sonic.

The architecture uses the following AWS services:

  • Amazon Nova 2 Sonic (through Amazon Bedrock): The speech-to-speech foundation model that powers Tara’s voice conversations. It handles both speech recognition and response generation in a single pass, supporting tool calling for structured data collection during the interview.
  • Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate: A serverless compute engine that runs the voice bridge containers connecting the telephony layer to Amazon Nova 2 Sonic. The voice bridge tasks run continuously across three Availability Zones for high availability.
  • Amazon Aurora Serverless v2: A PostgreSQL-compatible serverless relational database deployed in Multi-AZ configuration. Stores caller profiles, intake responses, qualification results, and session metadata. The serverless scaling of Aurora matches the variable call volume patterns.
  • Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic’s Claude 3 Haiku): Handles structured data extraction from conversation transcripts. After Amazon Nova 2 Sonic generates a transcript, Claude 3 Haiku extracts typed fields (names, dollar amounts, addresses, vehicle details) into the relational schema.
  • Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) with dead-letter queues: Manages asynchronous webhook processing for post-call events, preserving failed messages for retry.
  • AWS WAF, VPC Endpoints, and Application Load Balancer: Security and networking layers that help protect API endpoints, route traffic across Availability Zones, and provide private connectivity to AWS services.

Building and validating the voice agent

The team took a phased approach: validate voice quality first, build the production integration, then expand the questionnaire scope after proving the system worked with real callers.

Validating voice quality for sensitive conversations

Bankruptcy conversations are emotionally charged. Callers are often stressed, hesitant, or embarrassed. The voice agent needs to sound empathetic and natural, not robotic or transactional. Before writing any integration code, the team spent a dedicated week testing the voice quality of Amazon Nova 2 Sonic against several caller scenarios.

The validation covered:

  • Voice quality across caller emotional states (calm, stressed, hesitant, frustrated).
  • Time-to-first-audio latency benchmarks against the previous solution’s over 500 ms baseline.
  • Barge-in and interruption handling: can a caller interject mid-sentence without breaking the conversation?
  • Emotional tone adaptation: does the agent adjust its pace and tone when a caller sounds distressed?

This validation step produced a comparison report documenting the performance of Amazon Nova 2 Sonic against the previous solution across each dimension. The report became the go/no-go gate for proceeding to integration.

Deploying to production with real callers

With voice quality validated, the team built the end-to-end integration over three weeks. The call flow works as follows:

  • A caller dials the Bankruptcy.com number. Twilio’s telephony layer receives the call and opens a WebSocket connection to the voice bridge running on Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate.
  • The voice bridge streams audio bidirectionally between the caller and Amazon Nova 2 Sonic. Tara introduces herself, collects consent, and begins the intake interview.
  • After the call, the full transcript feeds into an extraction pipeline powered by Anthropic’s Claude 3 Haiku on Amazon Bedrock. The pipeline extracts the fields from the conversation and stores them in Amazon Aurora.

The full attorney-designed intake can run 15–20 minutes, which is longer than the maximum duration of a single Amazon Nova 2 Sonic streaming session (for the current value, see Getting started with speech-to-speech). The team treated that session duration as a design parameter and implemented the session continuation pattern, an approach that carries conversation context across session boundaries. The voice bridge tracks how long each bidirectional stream with Amazon Nova 2 Sonic has been open. Shortly before the limit, it opens a new stream with the same system prompt and tool configuration and sends the conversation so far as text history. When Tara finishes her current response, the bridge switches the caller’s audio to the new stream and closes the old one, so the conversation continues smoothly for the caller.

The initial deployment covered the existing 13-field intake form, collecting the same data points the web form captured but through natural conversation. This gave the team a production baseline to measure against before expanding scope.

Expanding the intake and lead qualification

With the production pilot running, the team expanded the questionnaire to the full attorney-designed intake over four weeks. This was a significant increase in scope:

  • Over 18 intake categories with conditional branching, where the questions Tara asks depend on the caller’s previous answers.
  • Complex relational data: Vehicles (year, make, model, financing status, monthly payment per vehicle), real estate properties, individual debt line items, multiple employment and income sources, and prior bankruptcy filings.
  • Rules-based lead sorting: Stretto applies attorney-defined rules to each lead, and attorneys make the final decision. Because a voice agent collects richer, conditional data than a static web form, it gives Stretto more flexibility to apply those rules and qualify leads accurately.
  • Lead routing: Qualified leads are routed to bankruptcy practitioners, while callers who do not meet the qualification criteria are directed to alternative resources.

The Amazon Aurora schema expanded to a full relational data model supporting one-to-many relationships. A single caller record might include four vehicles, two properties, and dozens of individual debt line items.

Measuring results and optimizing

The final phase focused on collecting production data and tuning the system based on real caller behavior. The team tracked key performance indicators including call volume, average duration, intake completion rate, profile completeness, conversion rate, and drop-off points.

Insights from production data drove several optimizations: reordering questions to reduce early drop-offs, adjusting conditional branching to collect high-value fields earlier in the conversation, and modifying qualification thresholds based on attorney feedback. The following table shows two key production metrics.

Average call duration (completed calls)~8 min
Data extraction accuracy~96%

Testing for quality and compliance

Deploying a voice agent that handles sensitive financial data requires more than functional testing. The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center (GenAIIC) advisory team guided the development of a comprehensive testing framework spanning four categories:

  • Happy path testing: Complete end-to-end intake interviews with cooperative callers across the full questionnaire. These calls confirm that the over 18 categories collect accurate structured data and that the qualification rules produce correct results.
  • Adversarial testing: Callers who provide contradictory information, change answers mid-conversation, refuse to answer certain questions, or attempt to manipulate the qualification outcome. The agent needs to handle the ambiguity and keep the conversation coherent.
  • Compliance testing: Consent collection, disclosure delivery, and data handling workflows. The team verified that the agent delivers disclosures accurately and collects consent before proceeding, because bankruptcy intake involves sensitive financial information.
  • Barge-in scenario testing: Callers interrupting at various points in the conversation, including during disclosures, mid-question, and during the agent’s responses. Tara should recover without losing context or asking the caller to repeat information.

Responsible AI controls in production

The team treated responsible AI as a production control, not only a testing step. Amazon Nova 2 Sonic includes built-in safety protections, described in the AWS AI Service Card for Amazon Nova 2 Sonic. On top of those, the solution keeps consequential decisions out of the model: lead sorting runs on explicit attorney-defined rules after the call, and attorneys make the final decision. Consent and disclosures are delivered and logged before intake begins, and the adversarial test suite checks that attempts to manipulate the conversation don’t change lead outcomes. Beyond model inference, the solution uses the Amazon Bedrock bidirectional streaming API for real-time audio, tool use for structured data capture during the interview, and private connectivity to Amazon Bedrock through VPC endpoints.

The GenAIIC advisory team also provided guidance on prompt engineering best practices for voice-specific applications, including techniques for managing conversational state across session continuation boundaries and structuring system prompts that maintain consistent agent personality across long interviews.

Results

After roughly three months in production, Stretto reported the following results:

  • Per-lead value: Fully qualified leads with complete intake data are significantly more valuable to bankruptcy attorneys than web form leads, which capture only a few basic fields.
  • Lead conversion: Stretto’s early production results show a 20 percent relative increase in conversion rate compared with the web form, even before the solution has been rolled out broadly across additional districts.
  • Data quality and call length: Stretto reports that Tara extracts structured fields at approximately 96 percent accuracy in its testing, and completed calls average about 8 minutes.
  • Voice solution cost: Stretto reports a 95 percent reduction in per-minute voice cost compared to its previous solution.
“I’m incredibly grateful to the AWS GenAI Innovation Center team. Their expertise helped bring our voice agent, Tara, to life, driving a 20 percent increase in our lead conversion rate.”
— Danya Gordin, Principal AI Architect, Stretto
“As one of the partners in the AWS Generative AI Partner Innovation Alliance, we can confirm that the GenAIIC program is a true catalyst, bringing customers and partners together to solve real problems and deliver business impact. With Stretto, that meant taking a voice agent to production in a matter of weeks and transform the bankruptcy intake process”
— Marcelo Wzorek, Executive Manager, CI&T

Conclusion

Stretto’s journey from web form leads to AI-assisted intake interviews illustrates what becomes possible when voice AI reaches the quality bar for sensitive use cases. By combining the speech-to-speech capabilities of Amazon Nova 2 Sonic with a well-designed architecture on AWS, the team built a voice agent that is natural enough for callers discussing personal financial hardship and cost-effective enough to deliver meaningful savings at scale.

The phased approach, validating voice quality first, deploying a minimal intake to production, then expanding scope based on real-world data, reduced risk at each step. The team built on validated assumptions rather than projections.

If you are exploring AI voice agents for your own use case, here are some resources to get started:

  • Learn about Amazon Nova 2 Sonic and speech-to-speech capabilities.
  • Get started with Amazon Bedrock to access foundation models including Amazon Nova 2 Sonic.
  • Explore AWS Fargate for serverless compute for containers.
  • Learn about the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center for advisory support on your generative AI initiatives.

If you are weighing voice AI for a sensitive, high-value intake process, your AWS account team and the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center can help you scope and build it.

About the authors

item.title: Reducing token costs and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore…
item.description: Full title: Reducing token costs and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore JSON workloads
item.content:encoded:
Reducing token costs and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore JSON workloads

As enterprises build production agents with dozens of tools and large structured inputs, token consumption and latency become the primary blockers to a good user experience. When these agents process large JSON data, every additional tool invocation injects the full payload into the large language model (LLM) context window, causing token usage and response latency to spike. Over multi-turn conversations, this pressure compounds, driving up costs and degrading response quality. Effectively managing context-window pressure in agentic systems is key to reliability and responsiveness at scale. In this post, we share three composable strategies we used to build a production agent for Flightscape that handles 20 MB+ JSON payloads. You can apply them to reduce token costs, lower latency, and maintain full reasoning capability across extended sessions. Together, these optimizations reduced token consumption by up to 71% and cut average latency by up to 80% across our benchmark runs on a representative 23 MB payload.

Solution overview

Flightscape is an airline operations platform that helps airlines plan and manage their crews, flights, and operations. As part of Flightscape’s crew management capabilities, we built a Training Schedule Optimization agent that verifies crew training schedule assignments against business rules. With 40+ tools and JSON inputs in megabytes, this agent could answer complex queries across crew assignments, scheduling, and resource allocation. Although the agent delivered the required functionality, average request latencies exceeded 15 seconds across most calls. Every tool call injected its full payload into the model context, inflating token counts and costs. On larger datasets, the context window filled up before the agent could finish reasoning. The following diagram (Figure 1) details the agentic architecture and data flow:

Figure 1: Agent architecture and data flow

In Figure 1, the Optimizer receives a Request JSON and produces a Response JSON, which is then validated by a Business Rules Validator to generate a Validation Report JSON. All three JSON documents are ingested by an AI Agent that provides a conversational interface for users to query optimization results, understand validation errors, and explore scheduling assignments. The agent is built with LangGraph, an open source framework by LangChain, and runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can be applied to validate and filter the agent’s conversational responses, helping facilitate responsible AI practices in production deployments. We defined a custom agent state that holds the data needed by our tools: optimization request JSON, optimization response JSON, and validation report JSON. We also added basic statistics and cache data to state for rich queries. The agent uses an Amazon Bedrock model for reasoning and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to persist chat interactions across turns, and each turn follows this flow (Figure 2):

Figure 2: Agentic flow

This is what the state structure looks like. The state references TOPT (Training Optimizer) request and response objects, which represent the crew scheduling inputs and optimization results:

class GraphState(TypedDict):
    """LangGraph state that combines messages with application data."""
    # Messages from conversation (managed by add_messages reducer)
    messages: Annotated[List[BaseMessage], add_messages]
    # Application-specific state - parsed domain objects
    request: Optional[TOPTRequest]
    responses: List[TOPTResponse]
    validation_report: Optional[Dict[str, Any]]
    basic_stats: Optional[Dict[str, Any]]
    cache_data: Optional[Dict[str, Any]]

Note: This state originally held heavy payloads inline. Later sections explain how we moved large artifacts out of conversational context to reduce token usage.

We implemented three strategies to reduce the token costs, latency, and memory overhead caused by passing large JSON payloads through the model context. The following diagram (Figure 3) shows how the three strategies fit into a single agent turn. Strategy 1 runs at the start and end of each turn, and Strategies 2 and 3 run each time a tool returns a result.

Figure 3: Overview of the three optimization strategies in one agent turn

At the start of a turn, the hydrate_state() function restores lightweight session state from AgentCore memory. When a tool returns an oversized list or dictionary, the agent stores the full result in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and passes the model a compact summary with a handle. The model can then retrieve more detail with get_result_page_tool(). At the end of the turn, the dehydrate_state() function writes heavy payloads to the S3ArtifactStore and saves only references to AgentCore memory. The following sections describe each strategy in detail.

Prerequisites

To implement these strategies, make sure the following are in place:

  • An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock and a supported model.
  • An Amazon S3 bucket for artifact storage.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory enabled for session-state persistence.
  • A LangGraph-based agent (or equivalent graph-orchestration framework) with tool-calling support.
  • A Python 3.12+ environment with boto3, langchain-core, and langgraph.

Optimization strategies

The companion code is available in this GitHub repository.

Strategy 1: Persist lightweight session state, offload heavy artifacts

Our first optimization was to change how we persist session state. Initially, large payloads were being stored too close to the conversational state. We therefore moved heavy artifacts (request JSON, response JSON, validation data, and other large derived payloads) to Amazon S3. AgentCore memory then persists only stable references to these objects, keeping the session state lightweight.

To support this, we introduced a dedicated persisted-state schema that keeps only lightweight fields and artifact references. The live graph state still includes parsed domain objects for tool execution, but persistence now writes a dehydrated form. At runtime, tools hydrate heavy payloads on demand using those references, instead of loading everything on every turn.

This PersistedState schema is what gets written to AgentCore Memory:

class PersistedState(TypedDict, total=False):
    """Serialized session state for AgentCore Memory.

    Heavy fields (request, responses) are stored in S3 and referenced by key.
    Lightweight fields are stored inline.
    """
    messages: List[Any]  # LangChain-serialized messages
    request_ref: Optional[str]  # S3 key for raw request JSON
    responses_ref: Optional[str]  # S3 key for raw responses JSON list
    cache_data_ref: Optional[str]  # S3 key for cache_data payload
    validation_report_ref: Optional[str]  # S3 key for validation_report payload
    basic_stats_ref: Optional[str]  # S3 key for basic_stats payload

The updated GraphState mirrors these references alongside the live domain objects:

class GraphState(TypedDict):
    """LangGraph state that combines messages with application data."""
    messages: Annotated[List[BaseMessage], add_messages]
    # ... (same domain fields as original graph state)
    # Artifact references for persistence
    request_ref: Optional[str]  # S3 key reference for raw request JSON
    responses_ref: Optional[str]  # S3 key reference for raw responses JSON list
    cache_data_ref: Optional[str]  # S3 key ref for cache_data payload
    validation_report_ref: Optional[str]  # S3 key ref for validation_report payload
    basic_stats_ref: Optional[str]  # S3 key ref for basic_stats payload

The dehydrate_state function strips heavy payloads from the live state and returns the lightweight persisted form along with the artifacts to upload:

def dehydrate_state(state: GraphState) -> Tuple[PersistedState, Dict[str, Any]]:
    persisted: PersistedState = {
        "messages": [dumpd(m) for m in state.get("messages") or []],
        "request_ref": state.get("request_ref"),
        "responses_ref": state.get("responses_ref"),
        # ... (remaining ref fields)
    }
    artifacts: Dict[str, Any] = {}
    if state.get("request_raw") is not None:
        artifacts["request_ref"] = state["request_raw"]
    # ... (see GitHub repository for full implementation)
    return persisted, artifacts

Rehydration reverses this process. When a session resumes, we rebuild the live graph state: deserialize LangChain messages, re-parse raw payloads into domain objects, and restore every reference key so later turns can locate their artifacts:

def hydrate_state(
    persisted: PersistedState,
    request_raw: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None,
    responses_raw: Optional[List[Dict[str, Any]]] = None,
) -> GraphState:
    """Reconstruct a live GraphState from its persisted form."""
    messages = [load(m, allowed_objects="messages") for m in persisted.get("messages") or []]
    request = TOPTRequest.from_dict(request_raw) if request_raw else None
    responses = [TOPTResponse.from_dict(r) for r in (responses_raw or [])]
    return {
        "messages": messages, "request": request, "responses": responses,
        # ... (remaining fields restored from persisted refs, see GitHub repository)
    }

Both dehydration and rehydration rely on the artifact store returning a consistent reference for each payload. Instead of minting a random key, we derive the reference from the payload itself. This approach, known as content addressing, serializes the JSON with sorted keys and compact separators, and uses the SHA-256 digest of those bytes as the reference.

The _content_hash helper produces a deterministic SHA-256 reference from a JSON-serializable payload:

def _content_hash(payload: Any) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(_canonical_bytes(payload)).hexdigest()

Content addressing makes writes idempotent. Identical payloads map to the same key, so a turn that re-serializes an unchanged request JSON reuses the object already in the bucket instead of uploading it again. The S3-backed store exposes a put_json and get_json interface. It also keeps a small in-process cache, so payloads already read or written during the current invocation do not require a second S3 round trip.

The S3ArtifactStore class wraps the put_json/get_json interface with an in-process cache and content-addressed keys:

class S3ArtifactStore:
    """Content-addressed artifact store backed by Amazon S3."""
    def __init__(self, bucket=None, prefix=None, region=None) -> None:
        self.bucket = bucket or os.getenv("SESSION_STATE_BUCKET")
        self.prefix = (prefix or os.getenv("ARTIFACT_STORE_PREFIX", "artifacts")).strip("/")
        # ... (boto3 session setup, see GitHub repository)
        self._cache: Dict[str, Any] = {}

    def put_json(self, payload: Any) -> str:
        ref = _content_hash(payload)
        with self._lock:
            if ref in self._cache:
                return ref  # Identical content already uploaded, skip PUT
            self._s3.put_object(Bucket=self.bucket, Key=self._key(ref), Body=_canonical_bytes(payload))
            # ... (cache update)
            return ref

    def get_json(self, ref: str) -> Any:
        with self._lock:
            if ref in self._cache:
                return self._cache[ref]
        # ... (S3 fetch and cache, see GitHub repository)

artifact_store = S3ArtifactStore()

Offloading heavy artifacts to S3 and persisting only lightweight references reduced per-turn latency and the volume of data stored in AgentCore memory. With heavy payloads no longer persisted inline, tool-call responses became the dominant consumer of context tokens, prompting us to introduce result paging.

Strategy 2: Page large result lists on demand

Even after moving heavy payload persistence to Amazon S3, we still had a major token bottleneck at tool-response time. Many tool results were too large, which created two problems. First, we were sending full lists to the model even when it only needed a small subset, making each turn slower and more expensive. Second, those full list payloads were injected into context, which quickly consumed the context window over multi-turn conversations.

In some cases, a single tool response exceeded 80,000 tokens, and the cost compounded as users continued interacting with the agent. We wanted to preserve full data access without sending everything by default. To solve this, we introduced on-demand result paging for large tool outputs. Instead of returning full lists, tools now return a compact payload with total count, a small sample, and a result handle.

When a tool result exceeds the sample-size threshold, the full list is stored in S3 and only a compact summary is returned to the model:

if len(result) > _LLM_SAMPLE_SIZE:
    handle = artifact_store.put_json(result)
    return json.dumps(
        {
            "_oversized": True,
            "_result_handle": handle,
            "total": len(result),
            "sample": result[:_LLM_SAMPLE_SIZE],
        },
        default=str,
    )

The handle points to the complete result stored in S3. When the agent needs more detail, it calls a paging tool with the handle and requests only the required slice, for example using offset and limit.

The get_result_page_tool function lets the model retrieve additional slices of a stored result by handle, offset, and limit:

def get_result_page_tool(handle: str, field: Optional[str] = None, offset: int = 0, limit: int = 50):
    payload = artifact_store.get_json(handle)
    if isinstance(payload, list):
        return {
            "handle": handle, "offset": offset, "limit": limit,
            "total": len(payload),
            "items": payload[offset: offset + limit],
        }
    # ... (dict field extraction, see GitHub repository)

On-demand paging kept the full list in S3 and served only the requested slice per turn, controlling context growth and significantly reducing token usage. However, not all oversized outputs were lists. Some tools returned large dictionaries that required a different compaction approach.

Strategy 3: Compact oversized dictionary outputs

Unlike lists, dictionary outputs contain deeply nested structured data that are useful for reasoning but typically too expensive to include verbatim on each turn. We needed a compact representation that preserved structural cues while drastically cutting the token footprint.

To solve this, we introduced descriptor-based compaction for oversized dictionary outputs. Instead of returning an oversized dictionary in full, we return a compact descriptor:

  • List fields are represented by count and sample.
  • Nested dictionaries are summarized by key count.
  • Scalar values remain inline where useful.

The full payload is stored in the artifact store, and the response includes a result handle. When the agent needs deeper detail, it uses that handle to fetch only the required data. This response format remained navigable for the model while significantly reducing unnecessary token usage.

The _oversized_descriptor function builds a compact structural summary of a dictionary payload, preserving field types and sample data without the full content:

def _oversized_descriptor(payload: Dict[str, Any], handle: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    fields: Dict[str, Any] = {}
    for key, value in payload.items():
        if key.startswith("_"):
            continue
        if isinstance(value, list):
            fields[key] = {"type": "list", "count": len(value), "sample": value[:5]}
        elif isinstance(value, dict):
            fields[key] = {"type": "dict", "keys": len(value)}
        else:
            fields[key] = {"type": "scalar", "value": value}
    return {"_oversized": True, "_result_handle": handle, "fields": fields}

If the serialized output still exceeds the character limit, the fallback stores the full payload and replaces the response with its descriptor:

content = json.dumps(llm_view, default=str)
if len(content) > _MAX_TOOL_CONTENT_CHARS:
    if handle is None:
        handle = artifact_store.put_json(full_view)
    content = json.dumps(_oversized_descriptor(full_view, handle), default=str)
return content

With lightweight persisted state, on-demand paging, and dictionary compaction in place, token growth became predictable and the agent stayed responsive even on multi-megabyte datasets.

Results

To validate the impact of these three strategies, we ran the same set of questions over the same dataset against both the pre-optimization and optimized versions of the agent. We then compared token usage and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability (a capability of AgentCore), and observed clear improvements in both cost and responsiveness.

Across a 5-question conversation run, total token usage dropped by approximately 71%, from ~289,500 to ~82,900 tokens, while average trace latency decreased by nearly 80%, from 15.4 s to 3.1 s (Figure 4). Across 100 sample questions (Figure 5), total tokens fell from 23.6 M to 8.5 M (64%) and average trace latency dropped from 7,930 ms to 2,461 ms (69%).

Figure 4: OTEL sessions comparison

Figure 5: OTEL sessions comparison across 100 sample questions

The effect was most dramatic on large single-turn payloads. Table 1 breaks down the per-turn impact for the heaviest single query (listing valid crews across every validation category).

MetricBeforeAfterReduction
Input tokens~32,000~8,00075%
Output tokens~2,80047783%
Turn latency~165 s9.9 s94%

Table 1: Input, output, and latency impact

Figure 6 and Figure 7 show the corresponding trace details before and after optimization.

Figure 6: Before trace detail

Figure 7: After trace detail

These gains came primarily from avoiding full payload injection into model context at every turn. Instead, the model now receives compact summaries first and fetches additional detail only when needed.

Figure 8: Compact summary event

The improvement was also visible in the trace timelines: the pre-optimization turn stretched to nearly 2 minutes 46 seconds, while the optimized turn completed in about 15 seconds (Figure 9).

Figure 9: Before and after timeline

The changes also improved behavior in longer conversations. Context growth became more predictable across turns, and the agent remained responsive even when users asked follow-up questions over large datasets. In practice, this shifted the system from compounding token cost to a more controlled, demand-driven access pattern.

Most importantly, these gains came without sacrificing capability. Full payloads remain in artifact storage and can be retrieved through handles whenever deeper inspection is needed. At Flightscape, this pattern provides a foundation for bringing conversational AI capabilities to complex airline operations workflows, keeping the underlying AI experience scalable and cost efficient.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources you created for this walkthrough:

  • Empty and optionally delete the S3 bucket used for the artifact store, or remove all objects under the artifact prefix (for example, artifacts/).
  • Delete any Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agents and associated AgentCore memory sessions created during testing.
  • Remove AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and policies created for S3 or Bedrock access.
  • Delete Amazon CloudWatch log groups generated by the agent runtime.
  • Remove any Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) endpoints or networking resources provisioned for this walkthrough.

Conclusion

If your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent handles large JSON data, start by identifying which tool outputs dominate your context window. Begin with offloading artifacts to S3 (Strategy 1) because it provides the foundation for the other optimizations, then add paging (Strategy 2) and compaction (Strategy 3) as needed to improve the token usage and latency of your agents. To get started, clone the GitHub repository and adapt the strategies to your own agent. To learn more about building agents with AgentCore and LangGraph, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation and the LangGraph framework documentation.

About the authors

item.title: Cut generative AI costs: Code for rules, models for judgment
item.content:encoded:
Cut generative AI costs: Code for rules, models for judgment

The biggest cost lever in a generative AI system is whether you call a model at all. We often see teams route every task through a large language model (LLM), including input validation, formatting, and routing. Each call is cheap in isolation, but at production scale these small costs become one of the largest line items in the architecture. Wherever a deterministic rule can do the job, skipping the model saves money, cuts latency, and removes a source of non-determinism. In this post, you learn how to decide whether each step in a workflow needs a model at all. You can then map each option to AWS: deterministic code, a constrained decision call, or a right-sized model on Amazon Bedrock.

Why unneeded model calls add up

The pattern usually starts in a prototype. A model call works for one step, so it becomes the default for the next. Those steps include validating input, reformatting a request body, and picking a route. At prototype volume, nobody notices the cost.

At production volume, unneeded model calls cost you in three ways:

  • Spend grows with request count, even for low-value steps.
  • Latency stacks, because every model call in a chain adds hundreds of milliseconds.
  • Output can vary, because the same input can return a different answer. That makes testing harder and audits slower.

Each new model launch then restarts the debate about which model to use. The earlier question, whether the step needs a model at all, goes unasked.

Cost guidance, including the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens, often starts at model selection. This post starts one step earlier: Does the step need a model at all?

How to decide whether a step needs a model

Figure 1 shows the whole decision as a flowchart with three labeled lanes: Runs as code, Questions, and Runs on a model. Take each workflow step through three questions in order, and stop at the first option that meets the step’s requirements:

  • Can a rule check success, such as a format, a schema, a keyword, or a range? If a rule settles only part of the step, a fast path runs the rule first.
  • Can a model write the rule once, such as a regular expression or a JSON schema?
  • Does the step pick one answer from a fixed list, such as a route, a class, or yes or no?

If the answer to all three is no, the step is open-ended and runs on a right-sized model.

Figure 1: Deciding whether a workflow step needs a model, and which one

Consider a customer support assistant. The following table shows how five of its steps go through the chart.

#StepPath through the chartWhere it runs
1Check an order number’s formatA rule can check success.Amazon API Gateway REST API request validation, or an AWS Lambda function
2Route a message by intentA rule settles part of it. A keyword match on the fast path resolves messages such as “refund”, and the residual goes to the third question.An AWS Step Functions Choice state that uses JSONata. The residual goes to a constrained decision call.
3Extract a tracking number from a carrier emailA model can write the rule once. It drafts a regular expression, and you review and commit it.Code, as a committed pattern in AWS Lambda
4Pick one of four support queues for a ticketThe answer comes from a fixed list.A constrained decision call. Unsure answers escalate to the right-sized model.
5Draft a reply to the customerThe task is open-ended.The right-sized model, the smallest Amazon Bedrock model that meets the requirements

You can use a model when a task is open-ended, ambiguous, or generative: summarizing a document, drafting a reply, extracting meaning from prose. Use deterministic code when the task has a checkable rule: an email format, a schema, an exact keyword, a numeric range. The following table shows what you trade away when you send a rule-shaped task to a model.

PropertyDeterministic codeModel call
Cost per invocationTypically orders of magnitude lowerPer-token, non-trivial at scale
LatencySingle-digit milliseconds or lessHundreds of milliseconds
Correctness on a well-specified ruleExact for the rule as writtenHigh, but with a non-zero error rate
AuditabilityThe rule sits in source controlHarder to explain to an auditor
Behavior over timeStable until you change itChanges when you move to a new model version, or when a version is retired

A model can also hallucinate and return different answers to the same input. A temperature of 0 makes varied answers less likely, but it doesn’t guarantee identical output. Amazon Bedrock model evaluation and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails help you measure and contain these risks. A rule has neither problem, which is one reason regulated workloads favor rules. A useful test: If you can write the acceptance test as a rule, you can usually write the step as a rule. For more information, refer to Orchestration models: From rule-based to AI-native in AWS Prescriptive Guidance.

Decide, don’t generate

Most routing and classification steps sit between a rule and open-ended generation. A rule can’t decide every case, but these steps don’t need generated text either. They need one answer from a fixed list of options that you define in advance, like the support queues in the preceding example. Use a component that limits its output to the allowed answers and gives you a signal for when to escalate. Confident answers proceed, and uncertain ones escalate. The AWS Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens describes this tiered, confidence-based escalation. On AWS, you can build it four ways:

  • A small Amazon Bedrock model with structured outputs – The answer is limited to an enum of options, plus an ‘unsure’ option that triggers escalation. This is the model’s own judgment, not a calibrated score, so check it against labeled data before you use it to decide escalation.
  • Embedding similarity – Embed the input with an Amazon Bedrock embeddings model and pick the nearest labeled example. Use the similarity score as an escalation signal, and set its threshold on labeled data.
  • Strands Decider, an experimental open source decision model under the Apache License 2.0 – It picks from options or scores against a rubric, and it returns a calibrated confidence with each answer. Its README reports that answers at a confidence of 0.9 or more are right about 95 percent of the time on short classification tasks. Because the model is experimental, validate that result on your own data before you use it in production. You host it yourself, for example on an Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint, by following the deployment guides in its repository.
  • A trained classifier on Amazon SageMaker AI – It returns class probabilities with low latency and cost once you have labeled training data.

The following JSON schema limits a structured-output answer to four queues plus ‘unsure’. Amazon Bedrock requires every object in the schema to set additionalProperties to false.

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "queue": {
      "type": "string",
      "enum": ["billing", "technical", "account", "other", "unsure"]
    }
  },
  "required": ["queue"],
  "additionalProperties": false
}

Whichever option you choose, check its escalation signal against your own labeled data, and set any threshold there. Keep your authorization decisions, such as a refund limit, in a rule.

The deterministic fast-path pattern

Many cost patterns focus on routing between models. The fast path goes one level earlier: Run the deterministic check first, and send only what the rule can’t settle to a model. Intent routing is one example. Many messages carry an unambiguous signal, such as “refund” or “reset my password”, which a keyword match resolves in single-digit milliseconds or less. If rules resolve 95 percent of requests, only 1 in 20 requests reaches a model, before any savings from model selection. (Illustrative arithmetic, not a benchmark.)

On AWS, you compose this from existing building blocks:

  • AWS Step Functions Choice states branch before the workflow invokes any model.
  • AWS Lambda hosts rules that need more than a Choice state, such as validation and schema checks.
  • Amazon API Gateway (REST API) request validation rejects malformed input before any compute runs.
  • A constrained decision call or an Amazon Bedrock model handles only the residual.

The following Choice state is a keyword fast path. It uses JSONata to send refund and password-reset messages straight to code, and it sends everything else to the constrained decision call.

"KeywordFastPath": {
  "Type": "Choice",
  "QueryLanguage": "JSONata",
  "Choices": [
    {
      "Condition": "{% $contains($states.input.message, /refund/i) %}",
      "Next": "RefundFlow"
    },
    {
      "Condition": "{% $contains($states.input.message, /reset (my )?password/i) %}",
      "Next": "PasswordResetFlow"
    }
  ],
  "Default": "ConstrainedDecisionCall"
}

You can also let a model write the rule once instead of running it every time. Have it draft a regular expression or a JSON schema, review it, and commit it. At runtime the rule runs at rule speed and cost. Review a model-written regular expression, and test it against known good and bad inputs.
