item.description: Full title: UAEF: A framework-agnostic system for closed-loop evaluation of AI agents
item.content:encoded:
UAEF: A framework-agnostic system for closed-loop evaluation of AI agents

Teams building AI agents on AWS use a range of frameworks, including LangGraph, LangChain, Strands Agents, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Each framework records agent execution in its own way, so the structure of messages, tool calls, and handoffs between agents differs from one to the next. Evaluation tooling tends to follow the same boundaries: teams build metrics, scoring logic, and result storage against a single framework’s trace format, and they must rebuild them when they switch frameworks or run agents on more than one.

This coupling makes a basic development question harder to answer: did a change to the prompt, model, or tools improve the agent? Answering it requires consistent metrics across versions of an agent and a shared record of past results to compare against. Agent quality also spans several dimensions that a single accuracy score does not capture: tool calling, response quality, responsible AI, performance, multi-turn conversation, multi-agent coordination, and reasoning.

In this post, we introduce the Universal Agent Evaluation Framework (UAEF). Customers across 12 organizations in the telecom, healthcare, and financial services industries used UAEF to evaluate their AI agents with one consistent set of metrics and compare agent versions before release. UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system: it uses adapters to convert traces from each framework into a common format, then scores those traces with 36 built-in metrics across 7 dimensions. It stores the results in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and generates reports and insights that inform the next iteration of the agent. This post describes how UAEF works, provides a playbook for choosing metrics and preparing datasets, and points to runnable notebooks for each supported framework.

UAEF: One evaluation layer for agent frameworks

UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system for AI agents. It takes the agent a team already has and scores it the same way across supported frameworks and runtimes. UAEF takes two inputs: the agent under test and a dataset to run it on. The dataset provides the inputs for each test case, and it can also include ground-truth answers, the expected output for each input. Ground truth is optional, and only metrics that compare the agent’s response against a reference use it. To evaluate tool calling, the ground truth must also include the expected tool calls for each test case: which tools the agent should call, in what order, and with what arguments. Everything after that happens inside the UAEF.

Figure 1 shows the path a single evaluation takes, from the inputs to the reports and insights. First, an adapter reads the agent’s native execution, its messages, tool calls, and agent-to-agent handoffs, and normalizes it into one canonical trace, so that the steps that follow are identical no matter which framework produced the agent. Next, UAEF screens the trace for personally identifiable information (PII), such as email addresses, phone numbers, and credit card numbers, before data is stored. The evaluation engine then scores the trace on a selection from 36 built-in metrics across 7 quality dimensions. When you persist a run, UAEF records it as an experiment in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3: Amazon DynamoDB holds the per-experiment metadata used for listing and comparison, and Amazon S3 holds the full results. With runs stored, a team can compare an agent version against a baseline to detect regressions and generate reports and insights that explain what changed and why. Those reports close the loop: the team evaluates the agent, learns what regressed or improved, changes the prompt, model, or tools, and evaluates again.

Figure 1: UAEF closed-loop evaluation data flow

The rest of this section follows that flow in order: the adapters that make UAEF framework-agnostic, the evaluation engine and its metrics, PII detection, experiment storage and comparison, and the reports that close the loop.

Canonical trace and adapters

Adapters are what make UAEF framework-agnostic. An adapter reads the record of an agent’s run, including its messages, tool calls, and agent-to-agent handoffs. It converts that record into one canonical representation called the AgentTrace, which is the only thing the rest of UAEF scores. Because of that conversion, UAEF works with the agent, whatever SDK it was built with (such as LangGraph, LangChain, or Strands Agents). It can run locally, behind an HTTP endpoint, or on a managed runtime such as Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with traces in Langfuse or not captured at all. UAEF provides an adapter for each of these, and they produce the same AgentTrace, so metrics, scores, and comparisons stay consistent across every one of them.

A trace reaches UAEF two ways. If one already exists, from a past run, a log, or an observability store, it is handed to UAEF and the matching adapter normalizes it. If not, UAEF invokes the agent for you: given a runtime Amazon Resource Name (ARN) or an HTTP endpoint, it calls the agent on each dataset input, collects the response, and adapts it in one step. Either way, the output is the same AgentTrace.

Because every metric, mode, and report operates on the AgentTrace rather than on a framework native format, the scoring that follows is identical no matter where the trace came from. That separation, normalization first and scoring second, is what lets a team compare an agent built on one framework against an agent built on another on a single scale.

Evaluation engine

The evaluation engine scores a canonical trace across 7 quality dimensions, each capturing a distinct aspect of agent behavior that a single accuracy number would hide. Tool calling measures whether the agent selected the right tools, called them in a sensible order, and passed valid arguments. Response quality measures whether the final answer is relevant, complete, accurate, and grounded in the provided context rather than hallucinated.

Responsible AI measures safety, bias, toxicity, and resistance to prompt injection. Performance measures operational cost in latency, token use, and throughput. Multi-turn measures how well the agent sustains a conversation, including context retention, coherence, and goal completion across turns. Multi-agent measures coordination in systems of cooperating agents, such as task delegation and the division of work. Reasoning measures the internal logic of the agent’s chain of thought, including consistency and freedom from fallacies.

Each dimension is computed by one or more of 36 built-in metrics, and every metric returns a normalized score in the interval [0, 1], where 1 is best, so dimensions and the overall result share one scale. Metrics come in two families. Deterministic metrics compute a score directly from the trace and the ground truth and reproduce exactly on repeated runs. Large language model (LLM)-as-a-judge metrics score qualities that resist a closed-form definition, such as response relevance or safety, by prompting a judge model on Amazon Bedrock. You can also add your own custom metrics or draw on the RAGAS and DeepEval integrations.

Because judge metrics feed an agent’s own output back into a prompt, that content is treated as untrusted input: an agent that can influence its judge can influence its own scores. The rubric is sent separately from the content, and the content is escaped so it cannot break out of its delimiter and be read as instructions. Each judge response is parsed strictly and must cite a verbatim span of the content it scored. A score whose evidence is not found is rejected rather than recorded. Judge scores are evaluation signal, not a safety decision, and should not gate a security control. For runtime enforcement on the agent itself, apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails in its own invocation path. The full model is in SECURITY.md.

Experiment management and comparison

UAEF records each evaluation as an experiment, so results from different agent versions can be compared later. Calling evaluate() or batch_evaluate() with persist=True creates a new experiment, identified by an optional name and objective, and writes it to two stores with complementary roles. Amazon DynamoDB holds one row per experiment with the metadata used for listing and comparison: evaluation count, the average score per metric, and an overall average. Amazon S3 holds a JSON file with the full evaluation results, including per-metric scores and the judge’s reasoning. Teams that handle sensitive data can turn on PII redaction for the stored copy.

The Python library also models a finer-grained structure. An experiment contains runs, and each run records the agent design under test: framework, model, tools, system prompt, and parameters. A run can also record a configuration snapshot and a Git commit. You can mark one run as the baseline for its experiment. This ties each score to the change that produced it, whether a new prompt, a different model, or an added tool.

Comparison works on the stored per-metric averages. For each metric that two runs have in common, the comparison engine calculates the absolute and percentage change. It then classifies the metric as a regression, an improvement, or unchanged, using a configurable threshold with a default of 5 percent. Several runs can be compared against a single baseline in one call. The regression detector also assigns a severity to each regression: minor (5–10 percent), moderate (10–20 percent), or severe (over 20 percent). It groups regressions by dimension, which shows, for example, whether a prompt change affected tool calling but not response quality.

In the web UI, the Compare tab lists stored experiments and filters them by framework or dataset. You select two or more experiments. The first is used as the baseline, and the UI shows per-metric scores with regressions and improvements highlighted. The UI calls the same library comparison engine, so results match what the Python API returns.

Report and insight generation

After an evaluation is stored, UAEF reports on it at three levels, each answering a different question. How did this run perform? Why did it score that way? How does it compare with earlier versions?

Results view. When an evaluation finishes, the web UI shows a summary of the experiment: the overall score, the number of test cases evaluated, the framework, and queries that failed to run. Per-metric averages appear with a dimension radar chart and a metric bar chart. A table lists every test case with its query, the agent’s response, the expected answer, and the score. Expanding a row shows the full response with its dimension and metric scores. For a multi-turn conversation, it shows each turn with its own scores and the tools the agent called.

Detailed report. From the results view or the experiment list, you can generate a statistical report on demand. UAEF loads the stored results from Amazon S3 and opens the report in a new browser tab. The report breaks results down by dimension and by metric. It shows confidence intervals and outliers for each metric, score distributions, correlations between metrics, a responsible AI summary, and test cases that reported failures. It closes with recommendations that point to the lowest-scoring dimensions and the metrics that vary most across test cases. The report is computed from the scores alone, without an LLM, so the same results produce the same report.

LLM-generated insights. In the Python library, you can pass a report to a model on Amazon Bedrock for analysis. For a single run, the analysis covers strengths, critical weaknesses, hypotheses about root causes, and prioritized recommendations. For a comparison of several runs, it covers the overall trend, likely causes of regressions and improvements, the risk each regression carries, and next steps. These insights suggest what to change in the prompt, model, or tools before the next evaluation.

Two ways to use it

You can run UAEF two ways over the same engine. With the Python library, you can evaluate agents in code from notebooks, scripts, and continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines. You can use the deployable AWS service to evaluate agents through a low-code web interface. You upload your dataset, select a framework and metrics, run the evaluation, and review the scores. Both paths run the identical evaluation engine and write to the same stores, so a result does not depend on which path produced it. You can start in the interface and move to code without changing how your results are scored or compared.

Evaluating agents with UAEF: A playbook

Knowing what UAEF can measure is different from knowing what you should measure. A travel-booking agent and a policy Q&A agent fail in different ways, and scoring both on every dimension wastes time and Amazon Bedrock invocations. Use this playbook to pick the metrics that match your agent, then add more as new questions come up.

Getting started

UAEF is open source under the Apache 2.0 license in the awslabs/uaef GitHub repository. It includes the Python library, framework adapters, built-in metrics, AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) infrastructure for the deployable service, the web interface, and runnable notebooks for each supported framework. The Installation Guide covers requirements, installing from a built package, and the development setup.

The service deployment guide covers deploying UAEF as a service with the web interface, the config reference, and teardown.

See it in action

A complete evaluation in the UAEF web interface, from ground-truth upload to per-dimension scores.

Choosing the metrics

Start from your scenario, not the metric list. Find the column that matches your agent and begin with the metrics checked in it. The Needs ground truth column shows which metrics compare against a reference answer or expected tool calls.

DimensionMetricNeeds ground truthScenarios
RAG / knowledge Q&AGeneral Q&ATool-using agentMulti-turn conversationReasoningSafety and complianceMulti-agentProduction monitoring
Response Qualityanswer_relevance✓✓✓
accuracy✓✓✓
completeness✓✓✓
hallucination_score✓
ragas_faithfulness✓
ragas_context_precision✓✓
ragas_context_recall✓✓
Tool Callingtool_selection_accuracy✓✓✓
tool_sequence_correctness✓✓✓
parameter_quality✓✓
mcp_compliance✓
Multi-Turncontext_retention✓
coherence✓✓
conversation_completeness✓✓
user_satisfaction✓
turn_efficiency✓
Reasoningchain_of_thought_coherence✓
logical_consistency✓
reasoning_step_correctness✓
fallacy_detection✓
Responsible AIsafety_score✓✓✓
toxicity_score✓
bias_score✓
prompt_injection_detection✓
Multi-Agentworkflow_completion✓✓
delegation_quality✓
agent_utilization✓
coordination_efficiency✓
Performancelatency_score✓
token_efficiency✓
cost_efficiency✓
throughput✓

The table shows recommended starting metrics for each scenario. For the complete list of supported metrics, see the metrics catalog.

Pass the metrics you picked as the metrics argument to evaluate() or batch_evaluate(). For a worked example, see the Example notebooks section that follows. Deterministic metrics, such as tool calling and performance, are computed directly from the trace, whereas others call an LLM judge. UAEF automatically skips metrics that need a reference answer when no ground truth is present, so partially labeled datasets and unlabeled production traffic are still worth evaluating.

Choosing the pipeline

Metrics decide what you measure. Six independent choices decide how the evaluation runs. Use the question in each row to settle it.

ChoiceAsk yourselfThen useIn code
Passive or activeDo I already have traces, or do I need to generate them under controlled conditions?Passive: evaluate a trace you already have. Active: call an invoke_* helper so UAEF runs the agent.evaluate(trace=recorded, adapter=“langgraph”) or raw = invoke_http_agent_for_framework( ENDPOINT, query, “strands”)
One trace or a datasetAm I debugging one case or measuring a release?Use evaluate() for one trace or conversation. Use batch_evaluate() for a dataset.evaluate(trace=trace) or batch_evaluate(traces=traces, max_workers=4)
Single-turn or multi-turnaDoes any test case depend on an earlier turn?Multi-turn: add session_id and turn_id to the dataset and pass every turn to the adapter, which assembles each conversation.sessions = adapter.transform_to_canonical( turn_payloads) batch_evaluate(traces=sessions)
Single-agent or multi-agentDoes more than one agent handle a single request?Nothing to configure. The adapter returns an AgentTrace or MultiAgentTrace, and UAEF selects the matching evaluator.adapter = get_adapter(FRAMEWORK) trace = adapter.transform_to_canonical(raw)
Offline or onlineAm I testing before release or monitoring production?Offline: a prepared dataset in development and CI. Online: live conversations, scored turn by turn.batch_evaluate(…) or OnlineEvaluator().evaluate_response( trace=trace)
Ephemeral or persistedbWill I compare this run with a later one?Persisted: set persist=True with an experiment name. Otherwise, use the returned result.batch_evaluate(traces=traces, persist=True, experiment_name=“Support agent v2”)

a Multi-turn – For details, refer to the multi-turn evaluation workflow guide.

b Only persisted runs can be compared.

Preparing your dataset

Provide one row per test case in a CSV or XLSX file. Only Question is required.

ColumnRequiredPurpose
QuestionYesInput sent to the agent
AnswerNoExpected response
contextNoReference documents for retrieval-style evaluation
expected_tool_callsNoExpected tool calls as a JSON array
session_idMulti-turn onlyGroups rows into one conversation
turn_idMulti-turn onlyOrders turns within a conversation, starting at 1

Question and Answer are matched case-insensitively and accept common aliases such as Query and Expected_Output, so existing test files usually work without renaming.

Multi-turn datasets. Rows that share a session_id are sent in order to a single agent session, so later turns can depend on earlier ones. Your agent endpoint must maintain its own conversation state, because UAEF sends each turn with its session ID rather than replaying history. Use lowercase session_id and turn_id. Otherwise, the file is evaluated as single-turn.

Protect sensitive data. Before sharing or persisting a dataset drawn from real traffic, use uaef.security.PIIDetector to detect and redact personally identifiable information such as email addresses, phone numbers, and credit card numbers.

Example notebooks

If you want to see more examples, check our notebooks/ folder. The notebooks cover scenarios such as batch evaluation, multi-turn conversations, multi-agent, and experiment management across frameworks including LangGraph, Strands Agents, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

NotebookWhat it covers
00_langgraph.ipynbLangGraph: single, batch, multi-turn, and multi-agent evaluation
02_langchain.ipynbLangChain agents
04_json.ipynbCustom frameworks, through the generic JSON adapter
05_strands.ipynbStrands Agents, including multi-agent
06_agentcore.ipynbAmazon Bedrock AgentCore, including multi-agent
07_langfuse.ipynbTraces already collected in Langfuse
01_langgraph_ragas_deepeval.ipynbRAGAS and DeepEval integrations
08_experiment_management.ipynbExperiments, baselines, and regression detection
10_reporting_pipeline.ipynbReports and dashboards from stored results
11_pii_detection.ipynbPII detection and redaction in traces

Clean up

Running the library creates nothing on its own, but persisting a run writes experiment metadata to Amazon DynamoDB and full results to Amazon S3. Delete both when you no longer need the saved experiments. The default names are uaef-experiments and uaef-results, overridable through the UAEF_DYNAMODB_TABLE and UAEF_S3_BUCKET environment variables. The bucket has to be emptied before it can be deleted.

If you deployed the service, the service deployment guide has the teardown sequence for both deployment modes. Read its retained-resources note before you assume teardown is complete: the DynamoDB tables, S3 buckets, and Amazon Cognito user pool are created with a retain policy, so deleting the stack leaves them, and their contents, in place. That is deliberate, so a teardown does not destroy saved experiments, but it means the storage keeps costing you until you remove it yourself.

Conclusion

UAEF separates agent evaluation from the framework that produced the agent. Adapters convert traces from LangGraph, LangChain, Strands Agents, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Langfuse into a common format, and a generic JSON adapter handles other frameworks. The same 36 built-in metrics across 7 dimensions then apply regardless of how a team built the agent. UAEF evaluates individual traces or runs batch evaluations over historical traces, then stores results per experiment in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3. Teams can then compare runs across agent versions, detect regressions, and use the generated reports and insights to decide what to change in the next iteration. The web UI and the Python library share the same evaluation engine, so teams can start low-code and move to code without changing how scoring or storage works.

To get started, see the open source repository.

About the authors

item.title: OpenAI Codex on Amazon Bedrock
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI Codex on Amazon Bedrock

Developers increasingly use Codex with Amazon Bedrock to explore unfamiliar code, make changes, and handle repetitive engineering work. For platform teams, the challenge is to make those tools available without creating a second model-access, identity, and operations stack.

Codex can use Amazon Bedrock for inference with supported OpenAI models. In this post, we show how to fit that path into the AWS identity, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), Regional, and observability practices your organization already uses. Codex still runs on the developer workstation. The main design choice is how its model requests reach Amazon Bedrock and where your organization applies policy and operational controls.

We begin with a small, least-privilege pilot and work through the checks that matter before access expands. The examples use GPT-5.6 Sol. Before starting the pilot, review Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock to confirm that Sol, Terra, or Luna is available in the AWS Region and inference path you plan to use.

Recommended default: Start with Native AWS Access for a small, least-privilege pilot. Choose AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, when you want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for routing or Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Choose an LLM Gateway when a platform team wants to enforce controls in the request path. A custom integration is the advanced version of the LLM Gateway pattern, not a quick start.

The examples come from the open source Guidance for Codex on AWS repository. It includes quick starts for Native AWS Access, AgentCore Gateway, LiteLLM on ECS, Portkey, the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT), and the Amazon CloudWatch setup used later in the post. Choose the quick start that matches your architecture, use it for the pilot, and adapt it to your environment.

Choose your rollout path

Authentication is only one part of an enterprise rollout. Decide who can use the service and which models and Regions are approved. Also define where configuration lives, what telemetry to collect, how usage is allocated, and which skills or Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers are allowed. The following table maps those needs to an access path and an owning team.

Choose the access path that provides the controls you need now. The most straightforward path that meets the requirement usually has the lowest operational overhead.

Decision rules

  • Native AWS Access is the usual starting point when AWS identity and IAM controls are enough for the pilot.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Within the platform, AgentCore Gateway fits teams that want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for routing, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, or related controls.
  • A large language model (LLM) Gateway fits organizations that already operate a gateway or want to enforce controls in the request path. Building a custom gateway is the advanced version of this option.

The following diagram compares where identity, routing, policy, telemetry, and operational ownership sit across the three rollout paths.

Figure 1: Codex runs on the developer workstation in each scenario. Native AWS Access uses AWS IAM Identity Center, a configured AgentCore Gateway can apply managed routing and Guardrails, and a configured LLM Gateway can apply request-path controls

Native AWS Access

If Native AWS Access fits the pilot, the repository’s Native AWS Access quick start provides the complete procedure and supporting files. The following abbreviated walkthrough focuses on the sequence and the checks that matter most.

Use your workforce identity provider for sign-in

Employees continue to sign in through the identity provider they already use. In this example, Okta handles authentication through Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) and provisions users and groups into IAM Identity Center through System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM). IAM Identity Center then issues the temporary AWS credentials used by Codex. The identity provider is not configured in Codex.

Prerequisites

  • Add each pilot user to a dedicated group in the workforce identity system and provision that group to IAM Identity Center. Keep the assignment limited to the pilot.
  • Choose an Amazon Bedrock Region and an OpenAI model available to the pilot identity, plus an inference profile if the selected API requires one. Check Sol, Terra, and Luna separately for the chosen account, Region, and inference path.
  • Grant only the Amazon Bedrock model inference permissions used by Codex, any direct validation commands, and the selected observability destination.
  • Prepare a non-production repository and name a rollback owner.

Configure

The pilot has three checks. First, sign in using the IAM Identity Center profile configured for the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and call Amazon Bedrock Runtime directly. Next, point Codex to the approved model. Finally, run a safe Codex task. The direct call isolates AWS access problems. The final step confirms the Codex configuration.

Step 1: Sign in and validate Amazon Bedrock Runtime access.

aws sso login --profile codex-bedrock
export AWS_PROFILE=codex-bedrock
aws bedrock-runtime converse
--model-id us.openai.gpt-5.6-sol
--messages '[{"role":"user","content":[{"text":"Reply with OK"}]}]'
--region us-east-2

This command creates a short-lived AWS session and checks whether the profile can invoke the chosen model in the chosen Region. If it fails, resolve the profile, Region, model or inference-profile access, or IAM permissions before configuring Codex.

Step 2: Configure the Codex provider.

# ~/.codex/config.toml (or managed user configuration)
model_provider = "amazon-bedrock"
model = "openai.gpt-5.6-sol"

[model_providers.amazon-bedrock.aws]
profile = "codex-bedrock"
region = "us-east-2"

The model value is the Codex model ID. The profile selects the AWS IAM Identity Center session, and region tells Codex which AWS Region to use. Keep these settings in user-level or managed configuration so a repository cannot change the provider.

Verify the pilot and confirm rollback

Before adding users, make sure the pilot reaches the approved model, produces the expected records, and can be disabled cleanly.

  • Identity: aws sts get-caller-identity returns the expected IAM Identity Center assumed-role session.
  • Model access: The pilot profile invokes the approved model through the API and Region selected for the test.
  • Codex access: The user completes a safe, read-only task in a non-production repository, and the expected request-path evidence is available.
  • Evidence and rollback: The identity, invocation, audit, and optional telemetry records are present. Remove the configuration or IAM Identity Center assignment, handle any active session according to your procedure or wait for it to expire, and verify that a new invocation is denied.

Watch the Native AWS Access walkthrough

The walkthrough shows the complete pilot sequence: workforce sign-in, direct Amazon Bedrock Runtime validation, Codex provider configuration, and a safe test task.

Figure 2: Native AWS Access walkthrough covering workforce sign-in, Amazon Bedrock Runtime validation, Codex provider configuration, and a safe pilot task

Use the video to verify the order of the checks and the evidence to collect before adding more pilot users.

Run a two-user identity-isolation check

Two users are required to test identity isolation. A single user shows that sign-in works. A second user tests whether attribution remains distinct. Have two pilot users sign in separately and run the same harmless task. Their assumed-role sessions and audit records, and telemetry records if configured, should remain distinct.

The following diagram shows how separate pilot identities should produce separate AWS sessions, request evidence, and optional telemetry while using the same approved Codex and Amazon Bedrock path.

Figure 3: Use trusted identity enrollment for attribution. A local collector can add approved identity context only when it is deployed and configured as part of a managed enrollment process

Gateway paths for request-path controls

AgentCore Gateway is an option when you want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for centralized routing or Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. If your organization already runs an LLM Gateway or wants to enforce controls in the request path, use that gateway instead. Validate the selected gateway before exposing it to pilot users.

LLM Gateway: Validate before a pilot

  • Check that the gateway accepts the Codex request format.
  • Use the sign-in or token flow defined by the gateway team.
  • Before inviting pilot users, test model routing, monitoring, failure handling, and rollback.

Custom enterprise integration

A custom enterprise integration is the most involved form of the LLM Gateway pattern. Consider it only when Native AWS Access, AgentCore Gateway, and an existing gateway cannot meet a specific requirement. The result is another service to design, secure, test, support, and operate, so platform engineering and security need to own it from the start.

Observe, govern, and allocate cost

Codex OpenTelemetry, Amazon Bedrock service records, AWS identity records, and billing data answer different questions. Codex OpenTelemetry describes client activity. Amazon Bedrock service metrics and model invocation logs show service-side activity when enabled. AWS identity records and the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) provide identity and billed-usage evidence. Correlate them for the path you deploy, and do not present token volume as a cost report.

Define what code, prompts, files, and tool output Codex might send through the selected model path. Exclude secrets and restricted data unless the organization has approved that data flow. Require developers to review and test generated changes before merge. Telemetry does not establish correctness or safety.

OpenTelemetry metrics from Codex

For observability, this post uses the ADOT collector configuration and CloudWatch dashboard from the repository’s monitoring and operations guidance. Deploy that configuration to each managed pilot device, then run a safe Codex task.

The repository provides the configuration files. Follow its deployment instructions to install the approved ADOT collector and configure its AWS authentication.

# ~/.codex/config.toml or managed user configuration
[otel]
environment = "pilot"
log_user_prompt = false
metrics_exporter = { "otlp-http" = { endpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:4318/v1/metrics", protocol = "binary" } }

Validate the repository path: run a safe Codex task and confirm that the expected operational metrics appear on the managed CloudWatch dashboard.

Telemetry planeExamplesAttribution boundary
Codex OpenTelemetry metricsToken usage, turns, API requests, request duration, tool calls, session source.Per-user and team dashboard grouping only after the local collector adds validated identity attributes.
Amazon Bedrock service metricsInvocations, latency, input tokens, output tokens, client errors, server errors.Use the documented namespace, metric names, and dimensions for the selected Runtime, Mantle, or AgentCore path.
AWS identity evidence, model invocation logs, and CURAssumed-role single sign-on (SSO) principal plus billed Bedrock line items.For Native IAM Identity Center access, CUR 2.0 with caller-identity allocation can expose the SSO principal. Gateway paths require gateway telemetry and spend records for end-user allocation.

Amazon CloudWatch dashboard and evidence

The Amazon CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights managed dashboard in the Guidance for Codex on AWS repository shows Codex operational metrics collected through ADOT. Use it to understand client activity, and use AWS identity, audit, and billing records separately when you need attribution or cost evidence.

QuestionDecisionEvidence to keep
Who invoked the model?Use the AWS identity/audit source for the path you selected.Pilot identity record and request correlation, where available.
What did it cost?Use billing data for actual charge and label any inferred allocation clearly.CUR source, allocation method, and known uncertainty.
Can we stop unsafe or expensive behavior?Use alarms for detection. Use IAM and managed client controls for their respective access and action boundaries. Use gateway policy when request-path enforcement, such as hard budgets or rate limits, is required.Control test results and rollback procedure.

Watch the Codex OTel and CloudWatch walkthrough

The walkthrough shows how to query Codex OpenTelemetry metrics and confirm that the expected token and request data appears in Amazon CloudWatch.

Figure 4: Codex OpenTelemetry metrics shown in an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard

The example validates the aliased metric result in Amazon CloudWatch Query Studio and shows how the dashboard represents Codex client activity.

Standardize team behavior

After the infrastructure path is working, turn to the developer experience. Repository guidance, managed plugins, hooks, and approved MCP servers can make the rollout consistent without asking each team to assemble its own setup.

Plugins

Organization-owned plugins are a practical way to distribute shared skills, hooks, and approved MCP integrations. Give each plugin an owner and version, review changes before release, and publish it only through approved sources. Test updates with a pilot group and keep a documented removal path.

A plugin might include an MCP server configuration, but that does not make every bundled tool approved. Allow only the servers and tools the organization has reviewed, with user confirmation where it is needed.

Hooks

Hooks can be declared in hooks.json or directly in configuration. Keep the documented event casing, and deploy organization-owned policy commands through approved endpoint tooling.

[[hooks.PreToolUse]]
matcher = "^Bash$"

[[hooks.PreToolUse.hooks]]
type = "command"
command = "/usr/local/bin/company-pre-tool-policy"
timeout = 30

Use PreToolUse, PostToolUse, or SessionStart where they solve a specific need. Before wider deployment, test allow, deny, timeout, and disconnected-endpoint behavior.

MCP

An MCP server connects Codex to another system, so each server creates a separate trust boundary. Limit access to the users and tools that need it, manage credentials through an approved OAuth or secrets process, and require confirmation for tools that change external systems. Keep MCP credentials out of the model-provider configuration.

Roll out in phases

The following diagram defines the scope and evidence required to advance from preparation through pilot, expansion, and organization-wide standardization.

Figure 5: Start with a controlled pilot, expand after validating the access path and operational evidence, and standardize the rollout after the operating model is proven

Administrator launch checklist

  • Record the selected path, owning team, Region, and model in the change record.
  • Limit the pilot identity to the required permissions, and document how issued credentials or tokens are handled.
  • Run a non-production test that covers sign-in, model availability, and one safe Codex task.
  • Check telemetry and audit output from the deployed version rather than assuming the example applies unchanged.
  • Separate billed amounts from estimates in cost reporting.
  • Exercise recovery: remove the configuration or assignment, handle any active session through the approved procedure or wait for it to expire, and verify that a new invocation is denied.

Clean up

When the pilot ends or access must be disabled, remove the rollout resources that are no longer required.

Remove the Codex model-provider and telemetry configuration from managed devices. Remove the IAM Identity Center pilot assignment or gateway access, revoke pilot tokens and secrets, and handle active sessions according to the approved procedure. Uninstall or disable the ADOT collector, and delete the pilot CloudWatch dashboard and alarms if they are not shared with another workload. Verify cleanup by confirming that a new model invocation is denied and that retired telemetry resources receive no new data.

Configuration boundaries

Keep model-provider, credential, and organization telemetry settings in user-level or managed configuration. Project-local .codex/config.toml is repository-scoped configuration: Review it as code, but do not treat it as an enterprise enforcement boundary. AGENTS.md is useful for durable repository guidance, such as test commands and coding conventions, but it is not an enforcement boundary either.

Setting typeRecommended locationReason
Model provider, credentials, RegionUser-level or managed configurationThese are endpoint and enterprise choices, not repository defaults.
OpenTelemetry exporterUser-level or managed configurationTelemetry destination and data handling are organization controls.
Repository instructionsAGENTS.mdCarries durable guidance but is not an enforcement boundary.
Permission requirementsOrganization-managed requirements.tomlConstrains supported security-sensitive client choices.

Conclusions and next steps

Codex can use Amazon Bedrock for inference with supported OpenAI models. Start with the least-complex access path that meets the requirement, prove the identity and model path with a small pilot, and add gateway or client controls only when they solve a specific need.

AgentCore Gateway provides an AWS managed gateway option for routing or Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Choose an LLM Gateway when a platform team wants to enforce controls in the request path. Build a custom integration only when the available paths cannot meet a documented requirement.

Expand in stages and use evidence from each stage to decide what comes next. The Guidance for Codex on AWS repository contains the maintained configurations and validation procedures used in this post.

About the authors

item.title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro on Amazon Bedrock
item.content:encoded:
Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro on Amazon Bedrock

Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed from Moonshot AI is now available on Amazon Bedrock. Part of Moonshot AI’s new K3.1 series, it’s a post-trained version of Kimi K3 with the same 3T-class open-weight architecture and 1-million-token context window, trained with substantially more post-training compute. According to Moonshot AI, that extra training targets long-horizon agentic work and fewer factual errors. It also improves professional tasks such as financial modeling and office documents, and coding for game engines, 3D scenes, and computer-aided design (CAD) scripts. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed generates output tokens at a higher rate and Moonshot AI reports 2–3 times the speed of Kimi K3.1 Pro.

Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed uses the same endpoint, APIs, and features as Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock. If you already build with Kimi K3, you can try it by changing the model ID in your existing code.

Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed supports tool calling, structured output, configurable reasoning, image input, and streaming. You can adopt Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed without changing your security posture. Your data is processed within the AWS data boundary, isn’t shared with Moonshot AI, and isn’t used to train the model. Zero data retention is always enabled for inference requests, and with zero operator access, AWS operators can’t view your prompts and completions during inference.

In this post, we show you how to get started with Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed on Amazon Bedrock. We also cover how to lower costs with the Flex tier, explicit prompt caching for repeated context, and how to use the model as a coding assistant in OpenCode.

Get started with Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed on Amazon Bedrock

To try the model without writing code, open the Amazon Bedrock console, choose Test, then Playground, and select Kimi K3.1.

From code, Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed is available on the bedrock-runtime endpoint through the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs, and through the Amazon Bedrock Converse and Invoke APIs. We recommend the Chat Completions API. You reach the model through cross-Region inference profiles:

  • global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 routes requests to any supported commercial AWS Region, and costs less per token than the geographic profiles. We recommend it for most workloads.
  • us.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 keeps processing within US Regions, and in.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 keeps it within India Regions, for workloads with data residency requirements.

Prerequisites

To follow the examples, you need:

  • An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock.
  • Python 3.11 or later, with the OpenAI SDK, aws-bedrock-token-generator, and boto3 installed (pip install -U openai aws-bedrock-token-generator boto3).
  • An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity allowed to call bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream on the Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed inference profiles. Add bedrock:CallWithBearerToken if you authenticate with a bearer token.

Call Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed with the Chat Completions API

If your application already uses the OpenAI SDK, point it at the Amazon Bedrock endpoint and change the model name. The following example creates a short-term bearer token from your AWS credentials and sends one request:

from openai import OpenAI
from aws_bedrock_token_generator import provide_token

REGION = "us-west-2"
MODEL_ID = "global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1"

# A short-term token derived from your AWS credentials, so no long-lived key is stored in code
client = OpenAI(
    base_url=f"https://bedrock-runtime.{REGION}.amazonaws.com/openai/v1",
    api_key=provide_token(region=REGION),
)

completion = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=MODEL_ID,
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a concise senior engineer."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "When should I prefer a queue over a stream?"},
    ],
    reasoning_effort="high",
)
print(completion.choices[0].message.content)

Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed always reasons before it answers. With reasoning_effort, you control how much: low, high, or max. If you don’t set it, the model uses max, so a lower value is the most direct way to reduce latency and output tokens on simpler tasks.

Call Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed with the Responses API

The same client works with the Responses API, which uses reasoning.effort for the same setting:

response = client.responses.create(
    model=MODEL_ID,
    input="Summarize the trade-offs between optimistic and pessimistic locking.",
    reasoning={"effort": "low"},
)
print(response.output_text)

Call Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed with the Converse API

If you already use the Amazon Bedrock Converse API, the change is the model ID:

import boto3

bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-west-2")
response = bedrock.converse(
    modelId="global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Explain idempotency keys in two sentences."}]}],
)

# The model can return a reasoning block before the answer, so pick the text block
content = response["output"]["message"]["content"]
print(next(block["text"] for block in content if "text" in block))

Lower costs with the Flex tier

The Flex tier serves Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed at half the Standard price, in exchange for potentially longer response times. It’s well suited to workloads where cost efficiency is a higher priority than response time, such as model evaluations, content summarization, and background tasks in agentic workflows. Because you choose the tier for each request, one application can mix tiers. For example, the same application could use Priority for latency-critical requests, Standard for everyday traffic, and Flex for cost-sensitive work. Your on-demand quota is shared across the Standard, Priority, and Flex tiers.

To use Flex, set service_tier to flex. The following example reuses the Chat Completions client from earlier:

completion = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=MODEL_ID,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "List edge cases to test in a function that parses ISO 8601 dates."}],
    service_tier="flex",
)
print(completion.choices[0].message.content)
print(completion.service_tier)  # The tier that served the request

On the Converse API, set serviceTier to {"type": "flex"} instead. To see how much of your traffic each tier served, use the ServiceTier and ResolvedServiceTier dimensions in Amazon CloudWatch. We recommend starting with a small share of your traffic on Flex and comparing latency and cost before you move more.

Optimize inference with explicit prompt caching

Agents and coding assistants resend the same large prefix on every turn: system instructions, tool definitions, repository conventions, and reference documents. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed caches repeated prefixes automatically, and with explicit prompt caching, you can mark where the stable prefix ends to improve your cache hit rate. Later requests reuse that prefix instead of processing it again, which lowers both latency and input cost for long, repeated context.

A few rules apply:

  • Explicit caching works on the Chat Completions, Responses, and Invoke APIs, but not on Converse.
  • A prompt_cache_breakpoint must follow at least 256 tokens of stable content.
  • Cached content is retained for at least 30 minutes.
  • Cache writes are billed at a higher rate than standard input. Cache reads are billed at a discounted rate and don’t count toward your input tokens-per-minute quota.

The following example caches a long system prompt and adds a second breakpoint after the user content, so a follow-up question on the same document can reuse both layers:

from pathlib import Path

LONG_STATIC_PROMPT = Path("repo_guidelines.md").read_text()  # stable content, at least 256 tokens
QUESTION = "Which of these guidelines apply to database migrations?"

def cached_text(text):
    # Marks the end of a cacheable prefix
    return {"type": "input_text", "text": text, "prompt_cache_breakpoint": {"mode": "explicit"}}

response = client.responses.create(
    model=MODEL_ID,
    extra_body={"prompt_cache_options": {"mode": "explicit"}},
    input=[
        {"type": "message", "role": "system", "content": [cached_text(LONG_STATIC_PROMPT)]},
        {"type": "message", "role": "user", "content": [cached_text(QUESTION)]},
    ],
)
details = response.usage.input_tokens_details
print(f"Cache read: {details.cached_tokens} tokens")  # greater than 0 on a cache hit

For more information, refer to Prompt caching for faster model inference.

Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed in practice: Coding with OpenCode

OpenCode is an open source, model-agnostic coding agent that runs in your terminal. You can connect it to Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed through the Amazon Bedrock Chat Completions API, using OpenCode’s OpenAI-compatible provider and an Amazon Bedrock API key. To create a key, open the Amazon Bedrock console in the AWS Region that you set in baseURL, then choose API keys. Short-term keys last up to 12 hours, work only in the Region where you generate them, and are recommended for production use. Long-term keys are intended for exploration.

Add the following to ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json, replacing the Region in baseURL with your own:

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "providers": {
    "amazon-bedrock-chat-completions": {
      "name": "Amazon Bedrock (Chat Completions)",
      "package": "@opencode/ai/providers/openai-compatible",
      "settings": {
        "baseURL": "https://bedrock-runtime.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/openai/v1"
      },
      "models": {
        "global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1": {
          "name": "Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed",
          "capabilities": {
            "reasoning": { "supported": true, "effort": ["low", "high", "max"] }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  },
  "model": "amazon-bedrock-chat-completions/global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1"
}

Start OpenCode in your project directory, enter /connect, choose Amazon Bedrock (Chat Completions), and paste your API key as shown in Figure 1. OpenCode stores the key, so you connect once per key. To switch between Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed and other models during a session, enter /models.

Figure 1: Connecting OpenCode to the Amazon Bedrock (Chat Completions) provider

The capabilities entry in the configuration lists the reasoning effort levels that the model supports, so OpenCode offers low, high, and max as variants of the model, as shown in Figure 2:

Figure 2: Reasoning effort variants for Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed in OpenCode

Output speed matters most in agentic coding. To complete a single task, a coding agent makes many model calls in a row. It reads files, plans a change, edits code, runs tests, and fixes what fails. Each call has to finish before the next one starts, and much of that time is spent generating reasoning and code. A higher output-token rate shortens every step, so the whole edit-test-fix loop finishes sooner and you wait less between iterations.

Availability

Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed is available on Amazon Bedrock through the global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1, us.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1, and in.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 cross-Region inference profiles. For supported Regions and model details, refer to the Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed model card and Regional availability. For pricing, refer to Amazon Bedrock pricing.

To get started, try Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed on the Amazon Bedrock console. To discuss your use case with the Amazon Bedrock team, connect with us.

About the authors

item.title: Build a daily dependency watcher with LangGraph and Amazon B…
item.description: Full title: Build a daily dependency watcher with LangGraph and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore web search
item.content:encoded:
Build a daily dependency watcher with LangGraph and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore web search

AI agents increasingly handle work that depends on what changed today, such as security advisories, product releases, prices, and regulations. A model’s training data can’t answer those questions, so agents need web search. For production use, teams also need results they can cite, and control over which sources count. They want search queries to stay inside their cloud environment because those queries often reveal internal work.

The Web Search API in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is now available. It gives agents and applications current web results through a single API call, signed with the AWS credentials they already use. AWS serves every query from a web index that Amazon operates, and doesn’t send it to a third-party search engine.

Each result includes the page’s title, URL, publication date, and an extract relevant to the query. Requests can include or exclude domains, and limit results to a publication date range. On AWS Lambda, Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), or Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, your agent calls the API with its execution role. There’s no search API key to store or rotate. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is also available through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. There, one administrator source policy covers every agent and Model Context Protocol (MCP) client.

For LangChain developers, the AgentCore web search tool in LangChain’s AWS integration now calls the Web Search API. One function call gives an agent current, cited search results. The tool can also hold rules that the model can’t change, such as a date window, a source blocklist, and a search budget. It returns its results as data that your code can check. It works with LangChain agents, with LangGraph, the orchestration framework that runs them, and with Deep Agents, which adds subagents, a virtual filesystem, and context compression.

In this post, you build a daily dependency watch for a security team as a LangGraph graph on the Web Search API. Every morning, the watch checks whether anything new affects the open source packages and container base images the team ships. It researches three package ecosystems in parallel, while your code keeps the date window, the blocklist, and the search budget out of the model’s control. It checks each finding against the sources it cites and remembers what it already reported. Then you run the watch on AgentCore runtime, and offer it across teams through AgentCore Gateway. In our test, the three branches finished in 36 seconds, against 99 seconds one after another.

Solution overview

The model decides what to search for and writes the findings. Every rule that must hold, whatever the model does, stays in code: the date window, the blocklist, the search budget, and the checks on each finding. Figure 1 shows how these parts fit together when you run the watch from the notebook.

Figure 1: A daily dependency watch with LangGraph and the Web Search API, run from a notebook

The numbered steps:

  • A run starts the graph with the watchlist and the watch window.
  • fan_out starts one research branch per ecosystem: npm, PyPI, and container base images. LangGraph runs the three branches in parallel.
  • Inside each branch, the agent calls an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock. The model decides what to search for and, at the end, produces structured findings.
  • The branch’s search tool adds the date window and the blocklist to each query. It calls the Web Search API with a request signed with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4). Steps 3 and 4 repeat, up to four searches per branch, in every branch at the same time.
  • Each branch keeps only findings that its sources support and that fall inside the window. When all three branches finish, LangGraph merges their findings and runs keep_new once.
  • keep_new checks the LangGraph store and records new findings, so nothing is reported twice.
  • report builds the cited table of new findings for the security team.

Prerequisites

Before you start, you need the following:

  • An AWS account, working in an AWS Region that offers the Web Search API. The examples use the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1). For other Regions, see Supported AWS Regions.
  • Python 3.10 or later.
  • AWS credentials for the identity that runs the notebook, from environment variables or an AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) profile. That identity needs the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permission from Step 1 and access to an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock.
  • The following Python packages: boto3 1.43.127 or later, the AgentCore Python SDK (bedrock-agentcore) 1.26.0 or later, and langchain-aws 1.9.3 or later. Install them with this pip command: pip install -U "boto3>=1.43.127" "bedrock-agentcore>=1.26.0" "langchain-aws[tools]>=1.9.3" langchain langgraph

Web Search and model calls are billed per use. For details, see Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing. One run of the watch makes at most 12 searches.

The complete code is in this notebook. The notebook runs every cell, including setup. The following steps cover the parts that matter for search.

Step 1: Grant the permission

First, give the identity you run as permission to search. The Web Search API needs one IAM action on one resource that AWS owns, so the statement is the same in every account. (For the full setup, see Grant permission to call the API.) This uses the same permission that a gateway’s service role uses for web search:

{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1:aws:tool/web-search.v1"
}

Step 2: Build a search tool with fixed rules

Now build the search tool that each research branch uses. The watch can’t let the model choose the date window, the trusted sources, or the number of searches. The graph also needs the returned sources as data, to check findings against them later. The web search toolkit in the langchain-aws package covers all of that with its options:

toolkit, tools = create_web_search_toolkit(
    region="us-east-1",
    exclude_domains=BLOCKLIST,
    published_after=window_start.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"),
    model_filters=False,
    max_searches=4,
    return_sources=True,
)

With no gateway argument, the tool calls the Web Search API. Every search carries the blocklist and the date floor, and a model’s own arguments could only narrow them. With model_filters=False, the model sees only a query argument. The tool stops after four searches, and it returns the results twice: as text for the model, and as an artifact for the graph. Each branch creates its own toolkit, so the branches search in parallel. You can give the same tools to a Deep Agents subagent.

Step 3: Define the findings schema

With the search tool in place, define what each branch returns. Each branch is a create_agent agent with a Pydantic schema as its response format, so it returns findings instead of prose. A finding has the package, a one-line title, and the CVE or advisory ID if the source gives one. It also has the severity that the source states, whether the source says it’s exploited, a recommended action, and the source URL. The notebook has the full schema and prompt.

Step 4: Build the graph and its evidence check

Now assemble the graph. fan_out sends one branch per ecosystem with the Send API in LangGraph, so the branches run in parallel.

Before a branch returns, code runs four checks on every finding. The checks compare the finding with what that branch’s own searches returned:

  • The cited URL came back from one of the branch’s searches.
  • The source’s title or text names the package as a whole word.
  • Any CVE or advisory ID in the finding appears in that text.
  • The source’s publication date falls inside the watch window. The artifact carries each date already parsed, and a missing date counts as outside.

After all branches finish, keep_new compares the surviving findings with a LangGraph store, and report builds the table. These checks catch an unsupported URL, a source that doesn’t name the package, an invented ID, and an out-of-window source. They don’t confirm severity, exploitation status, affected versions, or the recommended action. They also don’t prove when an issue was first disclosed: a page that the index dates this week can describe an older incident. For a production security workflow, verify findings against authoritative vulnerability feeds. Have someone review a finding before anyone acts on it.

Step 5: Run the watch

You’re ready to run the watch with a 7-day window. In our run, the three branches made 12 searches and got 80 sources back. They finished in 36 seconds of wall time, against 99 seconds for the branches added together. The evidence check dropped two findings: one whose source didn’t name the package, and one whose CVE ID didn’t appear in its source. None of the sources came from the blocked domain.

Four findings passed the checks, and keep_new reported two of them. Earlier test runs had already reported the other two, so the store held them back. Figure 2 shows the run in LangGraph Studio, the visual debugger for LangGraph. Every row of the report links to its source, which the Web Search acceptable use terms require for any output shown to users.

Figure 2: A run of the dependency watch in LangGraph Studio. The three research entries on the right are the three ecosystem branches, which LangGraph ran in parallel. The report lists only findings that passed the evidence check and weren’t reported before, each linked to its source

Step 6: Run the watch again to see only new findings

Finally, run the watch a second time to see the store at work. A scheduled watch runs every day, and the team shouldn’t see the same advisory twice. In our second run, the branches searched again and kept two findings, and the store had reported both before. So the report had nothing new, as Figure 3 shows.

Figure 3: A second run with the same input. The branches search again, but keep_new finds every result already in the LangGraph store, so the report has nothing new

For a scheduled job, swap InMemoryStore for a durable store with exact key lookups, such as DynamoDBStore from langgraph-checkpoint-aws.

Add web search to an existing LangChain or Deep Agents app

If you already have a LangChain agent, adding web search takes a few changes. Check these before you deploy:

  • Permission: add the Step 1 statement to the identity or execution role that your app already runs with. Nothing else needs to be created.
  • Region: the toolkit’s Region must offer the Web Search API, and it can differ from the Region of your model or the rest of your app.
  • Tool name: the tool is named web_search. If your agent already has a tool with that name, such as another search provider, set a different name on the tool before you add it.
  • Rules and budget: each toolkit carries its own filters and search budget. Create one toolkit for each agent or branch that needs separate rules or its own budget.
  • Throughput: all agents in an account share its Web Search quota, so parallel branches add up. By default, an account can send 10 requests per second in each Region. For details, see Quotas for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

With Deep Agents, you define the agent with create_deep_agent: a model, tools, a system prompt, and subagents. Pass the toolkit’s tools in a subagent’s tools list. Set the rules as toolkit options, because the tool applies them on every search, whatever the model asks. To check findings against their sources, as in Step 4, run that check on the agent’s output or add it as middleware. In our test, a Deep Agents coordinator delegated to a researcher subagent with these tools and returned a cited answer in about a minute.

Take it to production on AgentCore runtime

When you’re ready to run the watch every day without a notebook, host it on AgentCore runtime. Runtime runs agents built with any framework, including LangGraph, without a rewrite. It offers two compute types behind the same APIs. MicroVMs, the default, give each session its own isolated microVM, so one run can’t see another’s data. Instances run your agents on AWS-managed Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instances in your own account. They fit multi-day sessions, GPU workloads, or several agents that share one instance.

For the limits of each, see Use isolated sessions for agents and Runtime Instances and capacity providers. The Runtime sample next to the notebook holds the same graph as a Runtime entrypoint. Its policy grants the Runtime execution role the Step 1 permission and no broader access. Its README walks through creating, deploying, and invoking the project with the AgentCore CLI, on either compute type.

Figure 4: The same dependency watch hosted on AgentCore runtime. Steps 2 to 7 match Figure 1, with each search signed by the Runtime execution role. At step 1, a caller invokes the runtime, for example with agentcore invoke. At step 8, the runtime returns the report

Runtime session state is ephemeral, so the in-memory store lasts only as long as the session. A daily job needs the durable store from Step 6, invoked on a schedule.

Scale the watch across teams with AgentCore Gateway

The Web Search API and the Web Search Tool on AgentCore Gateway search the same index, and the same graph works on both. Choose by who enforces the rules and who calls search:

  • Use the Web Search API when your own application calls search and enforces its own rules, as in Steps 1 to 6. It needs only one IAM permission.
  • Use AgentCore Gateway when a platform team offers search to many agents or teams and wants AWS to apply one administrator source policy to every search. The policy sits on the gateway target, hidden from the agent, which can’t lift it.
  • Use AgentCore Gateway when MCP clients such as Claude need search, or when you want web search next to other tools behind one MCP endpoint.

The notebook’s optional Step 7 runs the watch through a gateway. It creates a web search target that carries the blocklist as an administrator policy, so the search client no longer adds it. This route needs two IAM grants on two different principals. The gateway’s service role needs bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch on the web search tool. The credentials your agent signs with need bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway on the gateway. Figure 5 shows the flow.

Figure 5: The same dependency watch through AgentCore Gateway. The graph is the same as in Figure 1. At step 4, the search tool calls AgentCore Gateway over MCP, signed with SigV4. At step 5, the web search target applies the administrator blocklist and calls AgentCore Web Search

To give each team its own policy, add one web search target per team, each with its own blocklist. This walkthrough notebook shows that pattern. For more on this route, see Web Search Tool.

Clean up

Steps 1–6 create no AWS resources. If you added the Step 1 permission only for this post, remove it from the identity you attached it to. If you ran Step 7, delete the target and the gateway to avoid ongoing charges. The notebook’s last cell does this when you set DELETE_GATEWAY = True:

target = gateway_client.get_gateway_target_by_name(GATEWAY_ID, "security-sources")
gateway_client.delete_gateway_target_and_wait(gatewayIdentifier=GATEWAY_ID, targetId=target["targetId"])
gateway_client.delete_gateway_and_wait(gatewayIdentifier=GATEWAY_ID)

The notebook leaves the gateway’s service role in place so other gateways can use it. Delete it in the IAM console when you no longer need it. If you deployed to Runtime, run agentcore remove all and then agentcore deploy -y from the project folder.

Conclusion

The Web Search API in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gives LangChain agents current, cited web results with the AWS credentials they already use. The dependency watch shows how to go beyond a single tool call. Keep the rules the model must not change in code, and keep the returned sources as data outside the model’s context. Check what can be checked, and keep the citations in everything users see. When more teams need the same search, AgentCore Gateway applies one policy to all of them.

To get started, open the notebook. For reference, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search integration page in the LangChain documentation and Search the web using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search.

About the authors
